docs.title: AI Agents Workshop
docs.text:
What You'll Learn

In this hands-on workshop you'll deploy an AI agent to IBM watsonx Orchestrate that helps doctors manage their patient portal inbox, and see why the naive version isn't safe to use. Across four labs you'll read the agent's traces, mask patient data, check the agent's work with judge agents, and work out who should be able to reach the data it touches.

docs.title: Which Model We Use
docs.text:
Your agent runs on Claude Sonnet 5.5. We use it because it's a high-end model at a reasonable cost. In our tests it returned concerns for all 12 patients and took about 40 seconds per patient.

In Orchestrate, the model is one line in the agent's definition (llm: in agent.yaml). Orchestrate's model gateway can route to many model backends, including open-weights models on watsonx.ai, so you can try another model by changing that line and redeploying. Run your checks again when you do: the first model we tried, gpt-oss-120b, often stopped after one tool call and missed concerns.

docs.title: Workshop Flow
docs.text:
1. Prerequisites: log in to IBM Cloud, run the installer, start the EHR inbox
  2. Slides: the AI Development Lifecycle, and the opportunities, risks and mitigations of agents in healthcare
  3. Lab 1: The Naive Agent: deploy the inbox agent to Orchestrate and see where it breaks
  4. Lab 2: Observability: read your agent's traces and mask patient data with a control and a plug-in
  5. Lab 3: Improving Your Agent: check the agent's concerns with three judge agents
  6. Lab 4: Securing Data Used By The Agent: find every copy of the agent's data and decide who can read it
Time Estimate

The workshop runs for 2 hours: about 30 minutes of presentation, then four labs of 15 to 25 minutes each.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Doctors are overwhelmed with patient portal messages. A single message might contain several unrelated questions. Some are urgent; most are routine. Responding to all of them comes on top of a full patient load.

Can we use an AI agent to help? And can we do it responsibly: keep the doctor in the loop, protect patient data, and resist letting the AI "just handle it"?

docs.title: Lab 1: The Naive Agent
docs.text: Deploy a background agent to watsonx Orchestrate. It reads a patient's record and portal messages and lists concerns in the inbox UI. It has no guardrails and no access controls, on purpose.

docs.title: Lab 2: Observability
docs.text: Orchestrate records a trace of every run without any code from you. Open a trace, find the patient data in it, and try two masking layers: the built-in PII Filter control and a Python plug-in.

docs.title: Lab 3: Improving Your Agent
docs.text: Learn how claim extraction, grounding checks, LLM-as-judge and a critic catch made-up evidence and off-task answers. Run three judge agents on Orchestrate against your agent's concerns and read their verdicts.

docs.title: Lab 4: Securing Data Used By The Agent
docs.text: The agent's output is patient data too. List every copy of the agent's data, check what IBM documents about how Orchestrate stores it, and discuss why access control belongs in the data layer and why the clinician's identity has to travel with every request.

The UI, the local EHR API and the lab agent service run on each student's laptop. The agent, its tools and the judge agents run on one watsonx Orchestrate instance shared by the room. Each seat deploys under its own name prefix, for example student0_, which scripts/ibm_cloud_login.py derives from the seat's username.

Patient data comes from one shared EHR on IBM Cloud Code Engine. Each seat gets a private copy of the 12 patients. The tenant ID is a SHA-256 fingerprint of the seat's API key, so the EHR never sees the key itself. The EHR saves each copy to IBM Cloud Object Storage, so copies survive server restarts. The local EHR API forwards to the shared EHR with the same tenant, so the UI and the agent's tools see the same data.

The agent's model is Claude Sonnet 5.5. Orchestrate registers it as an Anthropic model whose custom_host is the model proxy on the same Code Engine service. The proxy checks Orchestrate's token, swaps in the real Anthropic key, and forwards the request. The Anthropic key stays on the server; it never reaches the laptops or Orchestrate.

docs.title: Lab 1: The Naive Agent
docs.text:
Duration: ~20 minutes

What You'll Build

In this lab you'll deploy a naive AI agent to watsonx Orchestrate. The agent reviews a patient's record and portal messages and lists concerns for the doctor. You'll look at the files that define the agent, see how we get valid JSON out of it, and run it against real (synthetic) patient data.

In each step you run something and look at the result. By the end you'll have a working agent, a sense of what it does well, and a list of problems you'd want to fix before putting this anywhere near a real clinic.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Since the introduction of Electronic Health Record (EHR) portals, doctors are overwhelmed with messages from their patients. A single message might contain several unrelated questions. Some are urgent; most are routine. Responding to all of them comes on top of a full patient load — and that means keeping up is exhausting.

When patients don't get responses, important medical needs can go unaddressed.

A real inbox backlog

Dr. Sarah Kim works at Lakeview Family Medicine. The 12 patients in the workshop dataset have 26 portal messages that still need a reply. One is an urgent message from a patient whose pharmacy is refusing to fill their warfarin prescription. A later message from the same patient complains that nobody has replied.

How should Dr. Kim prioritize? Which messages need attention today, and which can wait? What patient history is relevant to each message?

docs.title: The Question
docs.text:
Can we use an AI agent to support doctor-patient communication outside of appointments in a way that:

  • Preserves the doctor-patient relationship — the doctor stays in the loop
  • Keeps the doctor as the expert — the agent surfaces information, it doesn't make medical decisions
  • Reduces cognitive load — the agent organizes and prioritizes, so the doctor can focus on the medicine
What we are NOT building

We are not building an agent that drafts responses for the doctor, makes diagnoses, or acts autonomously on patient care. That would be the Gmail "draft it for you" anti-pattern — tempting, but dangerous in a domain where the human must remain the expert.

Instead, we want the agent to surface and organize information so the doctor can act on it efficiently. Think "intelligent inbox triage," not "AI doctor."

docs.title: The Agent Loop: Observe, Reason, Act
docs.text:
Before you deploy anything, here's the loop every agent in this workshop runs.

Most agents today use a version of ReAct (Yao et al., 2023). It's a loop with three steps:

flowchart LR
    O[Observe] --> R[Reason]
    R --> A[Act]
    A --> O
Step What happens In our case Observe The agent takes in new information — a query, updated data, tool results A new patient message arrives, or the agent reads a patient record Reason The LLM decides what to do next — call a tool, ask for more info, or respond "This message mentions warfarin — I should look up the patient's medication list and recent labs" Act The agent executes — calls a tool, writes to memory, or produces output Calls get_patient_record(), reads the result, then summarizes findings

The loop repeats until the agent decides it has enough information to produce a final response. On watsonx Orchestrate, you don't write this loop. Orchestrate runs it for any agent with style: react_core.

docs.title: Chat agents vs. background agents
docs.text:
Most people encounter agents as chat agents — you type a message, the agent reasons and responds, you type another message. The user drives each turn.

But there's another pattern that's often a better fit for real systems: the background agent.

Chat agent Background agent Trigger User sends a message New data arrives (a patient message, a database update) Session User-driven, multi-turn Data-driven, often single-turn Ending User stops chatting Agent decides it's done UI Chat window Dashboard, inbox, notifications

For our doctor inbox problem, a background agent is the better design: incoming patient messages trigger the agent, it processes them and updates a structured inbox, and the doctor interacts with the inbox UI — not with a chat window.

Why not chat?

A chat interface is risky here because you can't stop doctors from asking the agent to draft responses, make diagnoses, or confirm medical correctness. An inbox UI keeps the agent's role constrained to organizing information, preserving the doctor's role as the expert.

Orchestrate gives every agent a chat preview. Anyone with access to your Orchestrate instance can chat with your agent there. The inbox UI only controls what doctors see. We come back to who can reach the agent in Lab 4.

docs.title: The Data
docs.text:
The workshop includes a set of synthetic EHR patient records. These simulate Lakeview Family Medicine, a small GP practice with three providers and 12 patients. The source files are data/patients/patient_001.json through patient_012.json.

During the workshop, a shared EHR server in the cloud serves these records. You have your own private copy of the 12 patients (see Prerequisites).

Each patient record contains:

Section Contents demographics Name, DOB, contact info, insurance, preferred language socialHistory Smoking, alcohol, exercise, lifestyle notes familyHistory Family medical conditions allergies Known allergies with reactions and criticality conditions Active/resolved conditions with ICD-10 codes medications Current medications with RxNorm codes, dosages, prescribers immunizations Vaccination records with CVX codes encounters Office visit notes in SOAP format labs Lab results with LOINC codes, values, reference ranges messages Patient portal messages with threading and priority How this data was generated

The synthetic data was generated using a structured pipeline designed to avoid common LLM pitfalls — see data/README.md for the full methodology. Key points:

  • A diversity matrix (data/patient_specs.json) was defined before generation to ensure varied demographics, conditions, communication styles, and clinical archetypes
  • Demographics were deliberately decoupled from clinical attributes — names and implied ethnicity do not predict occupation, condition, or communication style
  • Each patient was generated by an isolated subagent to prevent cross-patient pattern reuse
  • All medical codes (ICD-10, LOINC, RxNorm, CVX) are real

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lab, you will:

  • Understand the ReAct loop (Observe → Reason → Act) and where it runs on watsonx Orchestrate
  • Know which files define an Orchestrate agent and what each one does
  • Know the difference between an agent that surfaces information and one that generates content — and why it matters in healthcare
  • Know two ways to get structured output from an LLM: constrained decoding, and prompting with a schema plus validation and retry
  • Deploy the agent, run it against synthetic patient data, and find its runs in Orchestrate
  • Identify the limitations of a naive implementation

docs.title: Anatomy of an Orchestrate Agent
docs.text:
The Lab 1 agent is in lab1/agent/. Five files there define the agent, deploy it, and call it. The diagram shows where each piece runs.

YOUR MACHINE · lab1/agent/ agent.yaml instructions, model, list of tools tools.py Python @tool functions, uploaded as-is connection.yaml EHR URL and your tenant ID reads all three deploy.py adds your prefix to each name, imports connection, tools, agent agent.py asks the agent to review a patient, validates the JSON, retries once imports with the orchestrate CLI runs API WATSONX ORCHESTRATE (HOSTED) Traces one per run, with each LLM call and tool call you look at these in Step 4 Your agent ReAct loop, Claude Sonnet 5.5 calls tools Tool runtime runs your tools.py Connection EHR URL + your tenant gets patient records SHARED EHR (CLOUD) Lakeview EHR your copy of the 12 patients

Your agent and its tools run on Orchestrate, not on your laptop. Your laptop has the agent's definition files and agent.py, which asks the agent to review a patient. That's why you deploy before you run it, and why you look at Orchestrate's traces to see what the agent did.

docs.title: agent.yaml: the agent definition
docs.text:
This file defines the agent: its name, the model, the system prompt (instructions), and the tools it can call.

spec_version: v1
kind: native
name: lakeview_inbox_agent
style: react_core              # Orchestrate runs the ReAct loop
llm: virtual-model/anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5
instructions: |
  You are a clinical inbox assistant for a primary care practice. ...
  - Only surface information that is IN the record. Do not infer diagnoses.
  - Do not draft replies or make clinical recommendations.
tools:
- list_patients
- get_patient_record
- get_messages
- search_labs
- get_inbox

Read the full instructions in the file. You'll compare them with the agent's output in Step 5.

docs.title: tools.py: what the agent can do
docs.text:
Each function decorated with @tool from the Orchestrate ADK becomes a tool the LLM can call. The ADK builds the tool's schema from the type hints. The docstring becomes the tool description the LLM sees.

@tool(expected_credentials=EHR_CREDENTIALS)
def get_patient_record(patient_id: str) -> dict:
    """Get a patient's full record: demographics, conditions, allergies, medications,
    lab results, encounter history, messages, and social history."""
    resp = _get(f"/patients/{patient_id}")
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.json()

deploy.py uploads this file to Orchestrate as-is, and the tools run there. The file can't import anything else from the repo. _get reads the EHR URL and your tenant ID from the Orchestrate connection:

def _get(path: str):
    conn = connections.key_value(EHR_APP_ID)
    return requests.get(f"{conn['base_url'].rstrip('/')}{path}",
                        headers={"X-Tenant": conn.get("tenant", "")}, timeout=30)

The agent has five tools: list_patients, get_patient_record, get_messages, search_labs, and get_inbox.

Think about this

Notice that the agent can call list_patients() or get_patient_record() for any patient — not just the one it was asked to review. What could go wrong?

docs.title: connection.yaml: where the data is
docs.text: This file defines a key-value connection named lakeview_ehr. deploy.py imports it and sets two values from your .env: base_url, the address of the shared EHR, and tenant, the ID of your copy of the patients. Your tools read both values when they run.

docs.title: deploy.py: getting it all into Orchestrate
docs.text:
Everyone in the workshop shares one Orchestrate instance, and agent, tool, and connection names must be unique in an instance. deploy.py adds your prefix (WXO_NAME_PREFIX in .env, for example student0_) to each name. Then it runs three orchestrate CLI imports:

orchestrate("connections", "import", "-f", str(tmp / "connection.yaml"))
orchestrate("tools", "import", "-k", "python", "-f", str(tmp / "tools.py"),
            "-r", str(REQUIREMENTS), "-a", app_id)
orchestrate("agents", "import", "-f", str(tmp / "agent.yaml"))

Your deployed agent is named <prefix>lakeview_inbox_agent. Before the import, deploy.py also adds the output format to the instructions. See Structured Outputs.

docs.title: agent.py: asking the agent for a review
docs.text:
agent.py sends one message to your agent through Orchestrate's runs API. It waits for the run to finish, then checks the reply:

user_message = (
    f"Please review patient {patient_id}. "
    "Start by looking at their messages and record, then investigate "
    "any concerns you find. When done, output your findings."
)
text, thread_id = _client.run(user_message)

This is the only message it sends. The agent decides which tools to call.

docs.title: The output contract: models.py
docs.text:
The agent's reply must be a PatientConcerns object (in lab1/agent/models.py), which holds a list of Concerns. Concern is defined in app/models.py, the same model the inbox UI uses:

class Concern(BaseModel):
    id: str
    patient_id: str
    title: str
    summary: str               # one sentence
    action: str = ""           # what the doctor should do
    concern_type: ConcernType  # medication, lab_result, symptom, follow_up, administrative
    urgency: Urgency           # routine, soon, urgent
    status: ConcernStatus      # unresolved, monitoring, resolved
    onset: str
    last_updated: str
    evidence: list[str]        # specific values and dates
    related: RelatedData = RelatedData()  # links back to messages, labs, conditions, encounters

This is the contract between the agent and the UI. The agent fills it in; the UI renders it. The inbox never shows the doctor raw LLM output.

docs.title: Structured Outputs
docs.text:
No one reads the background agent's replies before they're saved. If a reply isn't valid JSON for PatientConcerns, the UI has nothing to show. There are two ways to get valid JSON from an LLM.

Some inference services offer constrained decoding, which works like this: you send a JSON Schema with the request. At each step of generation, the server masks every token that would break the schema, so the model can only pick tokens that keep the JSON valid. The output always parses.

Without that, we recommend prompt with the schema, validate, and retry. Lab 1 does it in three parts:

  1. Prompt with the schema. deploy.py generates the JSON Schema from the Pydantic models in models.py and adds it to the end of the agent's instructions. When you change models.py, the next deploy updates the prompt.

    spec["instructions"] += (
    "\nFINAL ANSWER FORMAT:\n"
    "When you have finished investigating, reply with ONLY a JSON object (no prose, "
    "no markdown, no code fences) that validates against this JSON Schema:\n"
    + json.dumps(output_schema(), separators=(",", ":"))
    + "\n"
)

  2. Validate. agent.py parses the reply with Pydantic. If the reply doesn't match the schema, Pydantic raises a ValidationError that lists each problem.

  3. Retry once. If validation fails, agent.py sends the error to the agent in the same conversation and asks for corrected JSON. If the second reply also fails, the run fails with an error and nothing is saved.

    except ValidationError as e:
    if attempt == MAX_FORMAT_RETRIES:
        raise
    text, thread_id = _client.run(
        "Your reply was not valid JSON for the required schema. Error:\n"
        f"{e}\n"
        "Reply again with ONLY the corrected JSON object.",
        thread_id=thread_id,
    )

Orchestrate's react_core agents don't offer constrained decoding, so Lab 1 uses prompt, validate, and retry. Here's a quick test you can run against our backend after you deploy your agent in Step 2:

cd ~/ai-agents-workshop
uv run python scripts/check_structured_outputs.py --patients 3 --skip-judges

The script sends your agent the same message agent.py sends, for patient-001 through patient-003. It validates each reply and retries once, the same way agent.py does. It prints one line per patient:

  • ok: the first reply was valid PatientConcerns JSON
  • ok (retry): the first reply failed validation, and the retry fixed it
  • FAIL: still invalid after the retry, with the validation error

The summary table counts 1st-try valid and valid after retry. Each line also shows how many tool calls the agent made. You'll need that number in What's Broken.

When we ran this on all 12 patients with Claude Sonnet 5.5, 10 first replies were valid and one retry fixed the other 2. Your numbers may differ.

Structured-decision models such as Jev have recently made a business of this, so constrained outputs may come back into the mainstream soon.

docs.title: Step 1: Explore the EHR Inbox
docs.text:
Before you deploy anything, look around the application. If the inbox from Prerequisites is still running, skip this command and switch to its browser tab.

cd ~/ai-agents-workshop
uv run streamlit run app/ui.py --server.port 8501

Open http://localhost:8501 in your browser.

This is Dr. Kim's inbox dashboard. Take a minute to explore:

  • Patient selector (top) — switch between patients. The emoji shows inbox status.
  • Medical record (left) — conditions, medications, labs, encounter history. Click the tabs.
  • Concerns panel (right) — empty for now. This is where the agent's output will appear.
  • Inbox (bottom left) — patient portal messages, newest first. Click one to see the full conversation.
Look at the inbox

Browse a few patients and their messages. Notice how some messages touch on multiple topics — a patient might ask about a medication refill and report a new symptom in the same message.

Now imagine you're Dr. Kim with a full day of appointments. How would you decide which messages need attention first?

docs.title: Step 2: Deploy Your Agent
docs.text:
Leave the inbox running. Open a second terminal and deploy the agent to Orchestrate:

cd ~/ai-agents-workshop
uv run python -m lab1.agent.deploy

The script prints each orchestrate command as it runs. It imports the connection and sets its values, then imports the tools, then the agent. The last line is:

Deployed. New tools can take a few minutes before the agent can call them.
The first few minutes after a deploy

Orchestrate sets up new tools in the background. For the first few minutes after a deploy, a tool call may return a message that the tool is still being configured. The agent's answer then won't make sense. Wait a couple of minutes and run the agent again.

This happens every time you run deploy.py.

Ask Bob

While the tools warm up, open lab1/agent/deploy.py in Bob and ask:

  • "What does deploy.py change in agent.yaml and tools.py before it calls the orchestrate CLI?"
  • "Where does the tenant ID that tools.py sends to the EHR come from?"

docs.title: Step 3: Run the Agent
docs.text:
In the second terminal, start the Lab 1 agent service:

cd ~/ai-agents-workshop
uv run uvicorn lab1.agent.api:app --port 8001

The inbox UI calls this service. When you click Run Agent, the service calls agent.py. agent.py starts a run of your agent on Orchestrate, validates the reply, and saves the concerns.

Now go back to the UI at http://localhost:8501:

  1. Select a patient from the dropdown
  2. Click Run Agent in the Concerns panel
  3. Wait for the agent to finish (the button will show "Agent Running…"). A run takes about 40 seconds, sometimes longer.
  4. Examine the concerns that appear
Try several patients

Run the agent on 2-3 different patients. Notice how:

  • Concerns are sorted by urgency (🔴 urgent → 🟡 soon → 🔵 routine)
  • Each concern has a specific action for the doctor
  • The Related links let you jump to the relevant message, lab, or encounter
  • The patient dropdown updates with urgency indicators

Write down which patients you ran and how many concerns each one got. You'll look at those runs in Step 4.

docs.title: Step 4: See It in Orchestrate
docs.text:
Orchestrate records a trace for each run of your agent. You didn't write any code for this. A trace shows every LLM call and tool call in the run.

  1. Open the watsonx Orchestrate UI for the workshop instance (the same instance the setup script found for you).
  2. From the main menu, open Analyze. You'll see a table of agents, including the other students' agents, because everyone shares the instance.
  3. Click your agent. Its name starts with your prefix, for example student0_lakeview_inbox_agent.
  4. Pick one of your runs from the list and open its details.

For each run, look for:

  • Which tools it called, in what order, with what arguments
  • The LLM calls between tool calls, and the final reply (the raw JSON before agent.py validated it)
  • How long each step took

Compare the run with the most concerns and the run with the fewest. How many tool calls did the agent make in each before it answered?

More in Lab 2

For now, just find your runs. Lab 2 covers traces in detail.

docs.title: Step 5: Evaluate the Output
docs.text:
Read the concerns for each patient you ran, next to the patient's record in the inbox UI.

Write down 2-3 things

For each patient you review, write down:

  1. Something the agent got right — a concern that's genuinely useful, well-evidenced, and actionable
  2. Something the agent got wrong — a concern that's misleading, vague, or incorrect
  3. Something that's missing — a real issue in the patient's record that the agent didn't surface

Keep these notes. We'll use them throughout the remaining labs.

Extra credit
  • Run the same patient twice. Do the concerns change? (The scripts/check_structured_outputs.py command above accepts --rounds 2.)
  • Open agent.yaml and read the output rules in instructions. Find a concern that breaks one of them.
  • Change the instructions to fix a problem you wrote down. For example, tell the agent to call search_labs for any lab value it cites. Redeploy with uv run python -m lab1.agent.deploy, wait a couple of minutes, and run the same patient again. Did the concerns or the tool calls change?
  • Ask Bob: "Read lab1/agent/agent.yaml. Which of its output rules could a program check automatically, and which need a person or another model?"

docs.title: What's Working
docs.text:
Some of this naive agent already works well:

Orchestrate runs the ReAct loop. The agent is a YAML file and five Python functions. Orchestrate calls the LLM, runs your tools, and records each step. The agent decides which tools to call.

Every reply is validated. The JSON Schema in the prompt comes from the same Pydantic model the UI uses. agent.py validates each reply and retries once with the error. Only valid PatientConcerns reach the inbox.

The UI keeps the doctor in control. The doctor clicks a button, reviews structured output, and acts on it. There's no chat box where they might ask the agent to draft a reply or confirm a diagnosis.

The agent runs in the background. It writes its concerns to a store, and the doctor sees them when they're ready. The doctor doesn't sit in a conversation waiting for each answer.

docs.title: What's Broken
docs.text: But this agent has serious problems. Some you probably noticed in your evaluation:

docs.title: 🔍 Nothing checks how much it looked at
docs.text:
The instructions say "Gather evidence before concluding." Whether the agent does depends on the model. get_patient_record returns the whole record in one call, so an agent can answer after one tool call without searching for lab trends or reading the rest of a thread. The first model we tried, gpt-oss-120b, often did exactly that and returned no concerns for some patients. Claude Sonnet 5.5 found concerns for all 12 patients in our tests, but nothing in the loop would tell you if it skipped something.

Check the tool calls in your traces. Lab 3 adds automatic checks.

docs.title: 🔓 No access controls
docs.text: The agent can access any patient's data at any time. When you ask it to review patient-001, nothing stops it from calling get_patient_record("patient-007"). In a real system, this would violate HIPAA's minimum necessary standard — the agent should only see data relevant to its current task.

docs.title: 🎲 Concerns aren't stable
docs.text: Run the agent twice on the same patient. You'll likely get different concerns: different titles, different urgency levels, maybe different issues. Each run overwrites the patient's previous concerns. There's no history and no way to see how concerns changed between runs.

docs.title: 🤥 No hallucination checks
docs.text: The agent might report a lab value that doesn't exist, misattribute a symptom, or fabricate evidence. Validation checks only that the JSON matches the schema. Nothing checks the values against the patient record. We're trusting the LLM to be accurate — and it won't always be.

docs.title: 👨‍⚕️ The agent may overstep
docs.text:
Read the instructions in agent.yaml carefully. They tell the agent not to infer diagnoses or make clinical recommendations. Check whether your agent's concerns:

  • Suggest diagnoses ("possible hypothyroidism")
  • Recommend treatments ("consider starting levothyroxine")
  • Editorialize on urgency in ways that could bias the doctor

Models are trained to be helpful, so they often add a likely diagnosis or a next step. In this inbox, that steers the doctor before they've read the record.

docs.title: 📋 No completeness checks
docs.text: How do you know the agent found all the concerns? It might surface 3 out of 5 real issues and you'd never know. There's no mechanism to verify coverage — no comparison against the actual record, no checklist, no second opinion.

docs.title: Up Next
docs.text:
Any one of these problems would stop a real practice from deploying this agent. The remaining labs work on them:

Lab Problem Approach Lab 1 No structure, no tools, just vibes A ReAct agent on Orchestrate with validated structured output Lab 2 No visibility into what the agent is doing Observability: Orchestrate traces, a PII control and a plug-in Lab 3 Shallow investigation, unstable output, hallucinations, overstepping Evaluation: claim extraction, grounding checks, LLM-as-judge, critic Lab 4 Unrestricted data access Security: who and what can reach patient data Keep your notes

The issues you wrote down in Step 5 are your personal roadmap for the next three labs. As we add observability, evaluation, and security, check whether each improvement addresses something you noticed.

Want to run it all on your laptop?

The open-source edition of this workshop builds the same agent with LangGraph. Everything in it runs on your laptop.

docs.title: Lab 2: Observability
docs.text:
Duration: ~25 minutes

What You'll Do

Lab 1's agent gives you concerns, but not how it got them. Which tools did it call? What data did it see?

watsonx Orchestrate already records this. Every run of your agent produces a trace. In this lab you'll open a trace, find the patient data inside it, and try the two masking layers Orchestrate offers. Then you'll compare traces to see what each layer changes and what it leaves alone.

Each step is something you run and look at. The extra-credit step at the end is optional.

docs.title: What an Agent Trace Needs to Show
docs.text:
Traditional software observability tracks status codes, latency and error rates. For an agent you also need the content: the prompts, the tool call arguments, the tool results and the model's replies. Without the content you can't tell why the agent said what it said.

The content also includes patient data. When the agent calls get_patient_record("patient-001"), the trace records:

  • Input: the patient ID
  • Output: the whole patient record: name, date of birth, phone, email, address, insurance member ID, medications, labs, messages

That output now lives in the trace store as well as in the EHR. The trace store is a second copy of patient data, and it needs the same rules as the first.

In the slides before this lab, we covered the "What to Log" framework:

Log Freely Log With Masking Do Not Log Latency, token counts Summarized user intent Raw credentials / secrets Model name, parameters Redacted inputs / outputs Full PHI in healthcare contexts Tool call names, success/fail Error messages (scrubbed) Internal API keys in tool args Trace structure / spans Session metadata Unmasked PII

Orchestrate writes the traces for you, so there's no instrumentation code to write or maintain. In exchange, the platform decides what goes in them. This lab shows what Orchestrate puts in its traces and which parts you can change.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lab, you will:

  • Find your agent's traces in Orchestrate and read a trace: LLM calls, tool calls, token counts
  • Find raw patient data (PHI) in a trace and say who can read it and for how long
  • Explain the difference between Orchestrate's model gateway, its controls and its plug-ins
  • Bind a PII Filter control to your agent and see what it masks
  • Deploy a PII masking plug-in and see what it masks, and what is still in the trace
  • Explain why returning less data from the tools is the only layer that keeps PHI out of the trace

docs.title: Step 1: Run Your Agent and Open Its Trace
docs.text:
You need your Lab 1 agent deployed, the inbox UI running and the Lab 1 agent service running. If you stopped them, restart them:

cd ~/ai-agents-workshop
uv run streamlit run app/ui.py --server.port 8501      # terminal 1
uv run uvicorn lab1.agent.api:app --port 8001          # terminal 2

In the UI at http://localhost:8501, pick a patient and click Run Agent. Write down the patient and the time.

docs.title: Find the trace in Orchestrate
docs.text:
Traces are in watsonx Orchestrate, not in watsonx.ai.

  1. Open the Orchestrate UI for the workshop instance.
  2. From the main menu, open Analyze. This opens Agent analytics, a table of agents.
  3. Click your agent, <prefix>lakeview_inbox_agent (for example student0_lakeview_inbox_agent).
  4. The Traces view lists runs with a timestamp, trace ID, status, model and latency. Pick the run at the time you wrote down.
  5. Open Trace details to see each step of the run.

IBM documents this path in Monitoring agents. The ADK docs describe the same data under "Analyze > [Agent name] > Overview and Conversations" (Observability SDK).

From the command line instead

The orchestrate CLI can list and export traces from your active environment:

orchestrate observability traces search --last 30m --limit 20
orchestrate observability traces export --trace-id <32-character trace ID> --output trace.json

search can't filter by agent name in the current ADK (that option is deprecated), so you'll see runs from the whole room. Use the time of your run to find yours. export writes the full trace as JSON.

docs.title: Read the trace
docs.text:
The trace is a tree of spans. One span covers the whole run. Inside it are:

  • LLM calls, with the model name (claude-sonnet-5-5) and input and output token counts. There's no cost figure.
  • Tool calls, with the full arguments and the full result.
  • The agent's final reply: the raw JSON before agent.py validated it.

Open the get_patient_record tool call and look at its output.

This is the patient record

The tool output holds the patient's name, date of birth, phone number, email, home address, insurance member ID, and the full clinical record, in plain text. The LLM calls that follow contain the same data, because the tool result is part of the model's input.

Orchestrate recorded all of it without any code from you.

Look at the run
  • How many tool calls did the agent make before it answered? Did it call search_labs or get_messages, or did it answer from get_patient_record alone?
  • Open the first LLM call and read its input. The "user" message was written by agent.py, not by Dr. Kim. The doctor never sees this prompt, but it shapes everything the agent does.
  • Compare what the tools returned with the concerns the agent wrote. Is every piece of evidence in the tool output? Lab 3 checks this automatically.

docs.title: Step 2: Who Else Can Read This Trace?
docs.text:
Go back to the agent list in Analyze. Open someone else's agent, for example the seat next to you, and open one of their traces.

You can read it. You can read their patient's record in the tool output.

That's because every seat in this workshop has the same broad role on one shared Orchestrate instance. IBM's docs say users with the Administrator or Builder role can view conversations in their tenant (Chat privacy and data protection) and that builders and administrators can view traces (Monitoring agents). The patients are synthetic, so this is safe today.

docs.title: Traces are PHI
docs.text:
Treat the trace store like any other copy of patient data. Data provenance means you can say where patient data went and what happened to it at each step. For the trace store, that comes down to three questions:

Question In this workshop Source Where does it live? In the Orchestrate instance, next to the agent. It is a separate copy from the EHR. Observed Who can read it? Every seat. Access follows the Orchestrate role, and every seat has a Builder-level role or higher. Tested; Monitoring agents How long is it kept? 30 days, then deleted. The period is fixed. Managing data retention

In a real deployment you'd answer the same questions before the first real patient: who gets a role that can read traces, whether 30 days fits your retention policy, and what the tools put into the trace in the first place. Lab 4 comes back to this.

docs.title: Policy Engines: What Orchestrate Offers
docs.text:
Orchestrate has three places where you can change what happens on the way into and out of your agent.

  • The model gateway routes the agent's LLM calls. It lets one agent definition use models from different providers: today it sends your agent's calls to Claude Sonnet 5.5 through the workshop's model proxy, which holds the Anthropic key so it never reaches your laptop. Model policies can fall back to another model, balance load across models, or retry (Model policies; public preview). Checking content is the job of controls.
  • Controls are Orchestrate's policy engine. A control binds a built-in policy type to your agent at a fixed hook, such as agent_pre_invoke (before the agent sees the message). Policy types include a PII Filter, Content Guardrails (jailbreak, hate/abuse/profanity, harm, social bias), Secrets detection, Regex pattern, SQL sanitizer, an output-length guard, rate limiters and model fallback/retry. (Managing controls)
  • Plug-ins are your own Python code, run at agent hooks such as agent_post_invoke (after the agent answers, before the caller gets the answer). (Plug-ins)

The diagram shows what we tested on the workshop instance. Content Guardrails and the other control types exist, but we haven't tested them.

Caller (agent.py) "Review patient-005" WATSONX ORCHESTRATE Controls agent_pre_invoke PII Filter: masks PII the user types. Verified. Content Guardrails: untested. Controls at tool_post_invoke and agent_post_invoke: accepted, but did not run in our tests. Your agent ReAct loop (react_core) LLM calls go to the gateway Tool calls go to the tool runtime Model gateway Fallback, load balance, retry to Claude Sonnet 5.5 Reliability only. Preview. Tool runtime runs your tools.py Tool output carries patient messages. This is the indirect prompt-injection path. No control inspects tool output. Plug-in agent_post_invoke Your Python. Masks phone, email, DOB and member ID in the answer. Verified. Trace store Every step writes here. Raw tool input and output, and the LLM context: this is PHI. Readable across the whole tenant. Kept 30 days. Answer to the caller concerns JSON Shared EHR (cloud) your copy of the patients

The injection path is the tool output

In this agent, untrusted text arrives through tool output: a patient's portal message, returned by get_messages or get_patient_record. The input controls see what the caller sends. The controls we bound to the post-invoke hooks didn't run in our tests, so in this workshop nothing inspects tool output. Until a tool-output control runs for you, handle it in your own design: return less from the tools (Step 5) and check the agent's answer against the record (Lab 3).

Here are the three layers for patient data, with what we measured:

Layer Mechanism What it protects What it doesn't protect Input PII Filter control at agent_pre_invoke PII the user types in the message. Regex detectors: phone, email, date of birth, SSN, MRN and others. Names. Anything that comes back from a tool. Output Python plug-in at agent_post_invoke Phone, email, labelled date of birth and member ID in the final answer Names and addresses. The tool output and LLM context, which are already in the trace. Source Tools return only the fields the agent needs The model's context, the trace and the answer Any field the tool still returns.

docs.title: Step 3: Bind the PII Filter Control
docs.text:
Bind the built-in PII Filter to your agent at agent_pre_invoke. Replace student0_ with your prefix:

orchestrate controls create \
  --artifact "PII Filter" \
  --name student0_pii_input \
  --hook agent_pre_invoke \
  --agent student0_lakeview_inbox_agent

The inbox UI always sends the same message, which has no PII in it. To see the control work, send your agent a message that does:

orchestrate chat ask --agent-name student0_lakeview_inbox_agent \
  "Please review patient-001. If anything is urgent, call me at 555-201-3344 or email dr.kim@example.com."

If orchestrate chat ask doesn't work against the workshop instance, open your agent in the Orchestrate UI and paste the same message into its chat preview.

Open the new trace. You'll see:

  • A control step at agent_pre_invoke before the agent runs, reporting that PII was detected and redacted.
  • The LLM input with the phone number and email masked.
  • The get_patient_record tool output, still with the patient's phone, email and date of birth in full.

The control cleaned what the user typed. It didn't touch what the tool returned.

The CLI also accepts this control at tool_post_invoke and agent_post_invoke. In our tests on this instance, those hooks produced no control step in the trace and masked nothing. That's why Step 4 uses a plug-in to mask the answer.

To remove the control later:

orchestrate controls remove --name student0_pii_input

docs.title: Step 4: Deploy the PII Masking Plug-in
docs.text:
Open lab2/orchestrate/pii_output_plugin.py. It's one function, mask_pii_output, marked as an agent_post_invoke plug-in. It runs regexes over the agent's final answer:

  • email addresses become [EMAIL]
  • phone numbers become [PHONE]
  • insurance member IDs become [MEMBER_ID]
  • dates of birth become [DOB], only when labelled ("DOB", "birth date"), so lab and visit dates stay as evidence

Redeploy your agent with the plug-in attached:

uv run python -m lab1.agent.deploy --pii-plugin

This imports the plug-in under your prefix and adds it to the agent's agent_post_invoke hook. Deploying again without --pii-plugin removes it. As in Lab 1, give a fresh deploy a couple of minutes before you run it.

We ran this plug-in live on the workshop instance with an earlier model. The --pii-plugin option of deploy.py has unit tests but hasn't been run live with Claude Sonnet 5.5. If you don't see the plug-in span in Step 4's trace, tell your instructor.

Ask Bob

Open lab2/orchestrate/pii_output_plugin.py and ask Bob: "Which of these regexes would match a lab date or a medication dose by mistake? Why is the DOB pattern written the way it is?"

Run the agent again from the inbox UI, on the same patient as Step 1. Then compare the new trace with the one from Step 1:

  • There's a new span for the plug-in, mask_pii_output (with your prefix), after the agent's last LLM call.
  • The answer that comes out of the plug-in has placeholders where the phone, email, member ID or labelled DOB were. If the agent didn't quote any of these in its concerns, there's nothing to mask. Ask for them with orchestrate chat ask (for example "include the patient's phone number in the summary") to see the difference.
  • The patient's name and address still appear wherever the agent wrote them. Regexes don't find names.
  • The get_patient_record tool span and the LLM calls still hold every value in full.

The plug-in runs after the model has read the full record, so it can only clean the answer.

docs.title: Step 5: Minimize at the Source (Try It Yourself, Extra Credit)
docs.text:
The input control and the output plug-in both leave the tool output in the trace. The only way to keep PHI out of the model and out of the trace is for the tool to return less.

get_patient_record returns demographics the agent never needs to find a concern: phone, email, address, member ID. The concerns are about labs, medications, messages and follow-ups.

Try it yourself:

  1. In lab1/agent/tools.py, change get_patient_record to drop the contact and insurance fields before it returns. The repository's data models already mark these fields with _pii and _phi in app/models.py. Use them as your list, but don't import app.models: tools.py is uploaded to Orchestrate on its own.
  2. Redeploy with uv run python -m lab1.agent.deploy.
  3. Run the agent on the same patient and open the trace. The tool span no longer holds those fields, so neither do the LLM calls or the answer.
  4. Check the concerns. Did the agent lose anything it needed?

Ask Bob for help: "Which fields in app/models.py are marked with _pii or _phi, and how would I drop those keys from the dict that get_patient_record returns in lab1/agent/tools.py?"

Lab 3 goes further: tools that search for one thing (a lab, a condition) instead of returning the whole record.

docs.title: What's Not Covered Here
docs.text:
Cost. Orchestrate traces show token counts per LLM call, not cost.

Custom spans. Tracing a hosted agent needs no code. For agents that run outside Orchestrate, IBM documents an Observability SDK and OpenTelemetry export (Observability SDK). We don't use them in this workshop.

Operational monitoring. In production you'd also track runs per hour, error rates and latency trends in your existing monitoring stack. The Agent analytics page shows some of this per agent.

Evaluation. Are the agent's concerns correct? That's Lab 3.

docs.title: What's Working
docs.text:
Every run is recorded. Every LLM call and tool call is in the trace, with inputs, outputs, timing and token counts, and you wrote no code for it.

Two masking layers you can see. The PII Filter control masks what the user types. The plug-in masks identifiers in the answer. Each one shows up in the trace as its own step.

You can say where the patient data went. The EHR, the model's context, the trace store, the answer. For the trace store, you know who can read it and how long it's kept.

docs.title: The trace still holds the full record
docs.text: Neither masking layer touches the tool output. Until the tools return less, every run puts a patient record in the trace store, readable by the whole tenant for 30 days.

docs.title: The agent still hallucinates and oversteps
docs.text: With the trace, you can compare what the tools returned with what the agent claimed, and see when it suggests a diagnosis. Nothing checks this automatically yet.

docs.title: The agent still investigates shallowly
docs.text: The trace shows how few tool calls the agent makes. Lab 3 adds checks for this.

docs.title: Up Next
docs.text: Lab Problem Solution Lab 1 No structure, no tools, just vibes A ReAct agent with structured output Lab 2 No visibility into agent behavior Orchestrate traces, PII controls and plug-ins Lab 3 Hallucinations, overstepping, shallow investigation Evaluation: grounding checks, LLM-as-judge, critic Lab 4 Unrestricted data access Security: where the data lives, who can read it, identity end to end

docs.title: Lab 3: Improving Your Agent
docs.text:
Duration: ~25 minutes

What You'll Do

In Lab 2 you read your agent's traces and compared the tool output with the concerns. Some concerns may cite evidence you can't find in the tool output. Some may suggest a diagnosis.

This lab covers how to check an agent's work: grounding checks, LLM-as-judge, a critic, and tools that return less. You'll read about each one, then run three judge agents on Orchestrate against your agent's concerns and read their verdicts in the traces.

docs.title: Where We Are in the ADLC
docs.text:
Lab 1 built the agent. Lab 2 made it observable. Lab 3 uses what you observed to improve what you built:

graph LR
    A[Run agent] --> B[Inspect traces]
    B --> C[Identify failure]
    C --> D[Implement fix]
    D --> A

This is the inner loop of the ADLC's Operations & Governance phase: monitor, find a problem, fix it, redeploy. Lab 2 gave you the inspect step. Lab 3 is about the check that comes before a fix: an automatic way to find the failures you were spotting by eye.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lab, you will:

  • Name the failures an agent check has to catch: made-up evidence, going off-task, shallow investigation
  • Explain claim extraction, grounding checks and LLM-as-judge
  • Explain how a critic and a revision loop use those checks
  • Run three judge agents on your agent's output and read their verdicts in Orchestrate
  • Name the limits of this check: what it's grounded against, and the same model judging itself

docs.title: What Lab 2 Showed
docs.text: Look back at your Lab 2 traces. Three kinds of problem show up.

docs.title: The agent can make up evidence
docs.text: Compare the tool output with the agent's concerns. An evidence string may cite a lab value, a date or a medication that isn't in what the tools returned. The agent states it with the same confidence as everything else.

docs.title: The agent can go off-task
docs.text: The instructions say "do not make clinical recommendations." The agent may still suggest a diagnosis, propose a treatment, or draft a reply. Its job is to organize what the doctor needs to see.

docs.title: The agent may not look far
docs.text: get_patient_record returns the whole record in one block. One call gives the agent everything, so it has little reason to search for a lab trend or read a whole thread, and every run puts the whole record in the model's context and in the trace. How often an agent answers after one call depends on the model: gpt-oss-120b often did, and missed concerns. Check the tool-call counts in your own traces.

docs.title: How to Check an Agent's Work
Claim extraction
docs.text:
A concern mixes specific facts ("TSH 4.8 mIU/L on 2026-04-01") with vague descriptions ("recent lab results"). A vague description passes any check, because it doesn't assert anything you can look up.

So the first step pulls out every specific claim. A model reads the concern's summary, action and evidence, and returns a list of self-contained claims: "Patient's HbA1c is 8.2%", "TSH trending up from 3.1 to 4.8 over 6 months". Internal IDs are replaced with what they refer to. Vague references are dropped.

The prompt is _EXTRACT_PROMPT in lab3/agent/grounding.py.

docs.title: Grounding
docs.text:
A grounding check takes each claim and the source data, and decides whether the source data supports the claim. The answer per claim is supported: true or false, with a reason.

The source data should be what the agent actually saw: the tool output from its run. A claim that's true in the full record but wasn't in anything the tools returned means the agent guessed.

docs.title: LLM-as-judge
docs.text:
The simplest grounding check is another LLM call: give a model the source data and the claims, and ask it to judge. This is LLM-as-judge. The prompt is _JUDGE_PROMPT in lab3/agent/grounding.py.

Its weakness is self-evaluation bias. If the judge is the same model as the agent, it has the same blind spots.

A purpose-built judge avoids this. IBM's Granite Guardian is a separate model trained to detect risks, including groundedness: given a context and a claim, it answers whether the claim is supported. IBM documents Granite Guardian on watsonx.ai. We haven't set it up for this workshop, so today's judges use the same model as the agent.

docs.title: Why one claim at a time
docs.text: A grounding model that answers yes or no for a whole concern can't tell you which sentence is wrong. With one verdict per claim, you get "TSH 4.8 is supported, but 'patient reported dizziness' is not." That gives the next step something specific to act on.

docs.title: The critic and the revision loop
docs.text:
A critic reads the concerns and the grounding verdicts and decides, per concern: is it on task, is it grounded, does it need revision? It returns feedback and an overall approved. The prompt is _CRITIC_PROMPT in lab3/agent/critic.py.

In a full loop, the feedback goes back to the agent, which revises its concerns, and the checks run again, up to a set number of rounds:

graph LR
    A[Primary agent] --> B[Extract claims]
    B --> C[Grounding check]
    C --> D[Critic]
    D -->|revisions needed| A
    D -->|approved| E[Save results]

We haven't built this loop on Orchestrate for this edition, so today you run the three checks on their own. There are two ways you could close it on Orchestrate:

  • From your code. Your code calls the critic agent, then sends its feedback to the inbox agent on the same thread. Lab 1's agent.py already continues a thread this way when it retries a bad reply.
  • As collaborator agents. The inbox agent calls the critic itself. IBM documents collaborator agents for Orchestrate; we haven't tested them here.

The repository's lab3/agent/ has the full loop for the open-source edition, written in LangGraph. Read it if you want to see one working version.

docs.title: Focused tools
docs.text:
Checks catch problems after the agent answers. Tool design prevents some of them.

If get_patient_record returns everything, the agent doesn't have to decide what's relevant. Compare tools that search for one thing:

@tool
def search_conditions(patient_id: str, keyword: str) -> list[dict]:
    """Search a patient's conditions by keyword (e.g., 'diabetes', 'hypertension')."""

The agent has to say what it's looking for: "the patient mentioned fatigue, so search for thyroid conditions and TSH labs." Each call returns less data, so there's less in the model's context to misread and less patient data in the trace. This is the same "minimize at the source" layer from Lab 2.

If you split the record into get_conditions, get_medications and get_labs with no keyword, the agent would likely call all of them and rebuild the full record. The keyword is what forces it to choose.

lab3/agent/tools.py has keyword search tools (search_conditions, search_medications, search_encounters) from the open-source edition. Your Lab 1 agent already has one: search_labs.

docs.title: Prompt injection
docs.text:
Patient portal messages are untrusted text, and they reach the agent through tool output. A message could include instructions aimed at the agent.

In this system the agent's output goes to the doctor. The patient never sees it, so an attacker gets no feedback on what worked. That limits the risk but doesn't remove it: injected text could still change which concerns the doctor sees. In Lab 2's tests, no control ran on tool output. The checks in this lab help here too: a concern that isn't grounded in the record gets flagged whatever caused it.

docs.title: Run the Judge Agents
docs.text:
Your Lab 1 agent should still be deployed. Run:

cd ~/ai-agents-workshop
uv run python scripts/check_structured_outputs.py --patients 3

This takes a few minutes. The script:

  1. Runs your agent, <prefix>lakeview_inbox_agent, on patient-001 to patient-003, the same way the inbox UI does.
  2. Creates (or updates) three small agents on Orchestrate, with no tools, under your prefix: <prefix>claim_extractor, <prefix>grounding_judge and <prefix>critic. Their instructions are the Lab 3 prompts above, plus the JSON format each one must reply in.
  3. For each patient, takes up to three of your agent's concerns and sends each one to the claim extractor, then sends the claims to the grounding judge.
  4. Sends all of the patient's concerns and the verdicts to the critic.

All four agents use the same model, Claude Sonnet 5.5.

Ask Bob

While it runs, open scripts/check_structured_outputs.py and ask Bob: "What does deploy_judges send to Orchestrate, and where do the judges' instructions come from?"

docs.title: What you'll see in the terminal
docs.text:
One line per step. Yours will have different titles, timings and counts:

Main agent: student0_lakeview_inbox_agent (3 patients x 1 round(s))
  patient-001 r1: ok 21s, 1 tool calls, 4 concerns
  ...
Deployed judge agents: student0_claim_extractor, student0_grounding_judge, student0_critic

Grounding + critic on 3 patients (up to 3 concerns each)
  extraction patient-001 Rising TSH with new tachy: ok 6s
  judge      patient-001 Rising TSH with new tachy: ok 9s
  ...
  critic     patient-001: ok 12s

ok means the reply was valid JSON for that step's schema. ok (retry) means the first reply wasn't and one retry fixed it. FAIL means it was still invalid. The summary table at the end counts these per step.

The terminal shows whether each judge answered in the right format. It doesn't print what they decided. For that, open the traces.

docs.title: What you'll see in Orchestrate
docs.text:
In Analyze, open each judge agent and look at its most recent traces, the same way you did in Lab 2.

  • <prefix>claim_extractor: the input is one concern. The output is a list of claims. Did it drop anything specific? Did it keep anything vague?
  • <prefix>grounding_judge: the input is the patient's record and the claims. The output is one verdict per claim, supported with a reason. Look for supported: false. Then check the record yourself: is the judge right?
  • <prefix>critic: the output has, per concern, on_task, grounded, revision_needed and feedback, plus an overall approved and summary. Did the critic flag the concerns you'd flag? Did it flag anything for suggesting a diagnosis?
Two limits of this check

It's grounded against the full record. The script sends the judge the patient's whole EHR record (cut to 60,000 characters), not the tool output from your agent's run. A claim can be supported by the record even though your agent never fetched that data. This check catches claims that aren't true. It doesn't catch claims the agent made without looking.

The same model judges itself. The agent and all three judges run on Claude Sonnet 5.5. A mistake the model tends to make as the agent, it may also accept as the judge. A purpose-built judge such as Granite Guardian is one way around this. It isn't available in this edition.

Things to notice
  1. How many concerns had at least one supported: false claim? When you check them by hand, are they real mistakes?
  2. Did the critic approve every patient? If it did, read its feedback. Is it checking anything, or agreeing?
  3. Run it twice (--rounds 2 re-runs your agent; the judges run on the first round). Do the verdicts change?
Extra credit
  • Read _JUDGE_PROMPT and _CRITIC_PROMPT in lab3/. Find an instruction the judge or critic didn't follow in your traces.
  • Tighten the critic. Add a rule to _CRITIC_PROMPT in lab3/agent/critic.py, for example "Flag any concern whose action recommends a treatment." Keep the CONCERNS: line and everything below it. Run the script again: it redeploys the judge agents from the prompts each time. Did the critic's verdicts change?
  • In scripts/check_structured_outputs.py, find where the judge's source data is built (search for SOURCE DATA). What would you need from Lab 2's traces to ground against the tool output instead?
  • Write down how you'd wire the critic's feedback back into your agent. Your Lab 1 agent.py already continues a conversation by thread_id when it retries a bad reply.

docs.title: What's Working
docs.text:
Each check is a small agent with one job. The extractor, the judge and the critic each have one prompt and one output schema. You can read each one's input and output in its own trace.

Verdicts are per claim. When the judge rejects something, you know which fact it rejected and why.

The checks use structured output. Every verdict is validated against a schema, so a program can act on it: count failures, route a concern back for revision, or hold it from the inbox.

Where Orchestrate evaluations and watsonx.governance fit

Today's judges are agents you deploy yourself, so you can read every prompt and verdict. IBM documents tools for the same job, which we haven't tested in this workshop:

  • The ADK's orchestrate evaluations commands run test cases against an agent and check which tools it called and in what order (Evaluations).
  • The watsonx.governance SDK, ibm-watsonx-gov, has metrics such as faithfulness, answer relevance and tool-call accuracy (ibm-watsonx-gov).
  • watsonx.governance keeps a record of each AI use case and its evaluation results, which is what an auditor asks for.

docs.title: What's Still Broken
docs.text:
The loop isn't closed. The critic's feedback doesn't go back to your agent. Nothing gets revised.

The check is weaker than it looks. It grounds against the full record, and the same model judges its own kind of output.

The agent still has unrestricted access. Any tool can fetch any patient's record. There's no record of who asked for what, and no identity attached to the request. That's Lab 4.

docs.title: 🔒 Lab 4: Securing Data Used By The Agent
Lab 4: Securing Data Used By The Agent
docs.text:
Duration: ~15 minutes

What You'll Cover

Your agent reads patient records and writes concerns about them. Copies of that data now exist in several places: the EHR, the model's context, Orchestrate's traces, and the concerns file on your laptop.

This lab is a discussion with one short look at a trace. There's no code to change. You'll list where the agent's data lives, check what IBM documents about how watsonx Orchestrate stores it, and work through who should be able to read each copy. Then you'll look at why access rules belong in the data layer, and why the clinician's identity has to travel with every request.

docs.title: Where We Are in the ADLC
docs.text: Lab 1 built the agent. Lab 2 made it observable. Lab 3 checked its work. Lab 4 is Governance: making sure every copy of the data the agent touches is protected as well as the original.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lab, you will:

  • List every place this agent's data is stored or processed, and who can read each one
  • Say what IBM documents about storage on watsonx Orchestrate (region, encryption, isolation, retention, compliance) and what it doesn't
  • Explain why an agent's output is PHI that needs the same protection as its input
  • Explain why access control belongs in the data layer, not in the prompt or the UI
  • Explain how keeping the clinician's identity attached end to end limits what the agent can fetch
  • Find, in a trace, where your agent's tools return data about every patient

docs.title: Agent Output Is Sensitive Data
docs.text:
A concern like "INR trending up while the patient reports missed warfarin doses" names a medication, a lab result, and something the patient told their doctor. Anyone who reads it learns about that patient's health. The agent derived new PHI from several records.

In this workshop, concerns go to a JSON file on your laptop. Any code path can read or overwrite any patient's concerns, nothing records who looked, and running the agent again replaces the previous output. That's acceptable only because the patients are synthetic.

A real practice has a second problem. Dr. Kim and Rachel Torres may both run the agent on the same patient and get different concerns. Each set belongs to the clinician who asked for it. The agent acts as their delegate, so access to its output should follow the same rules as access to the patient's chart.

docs.title: Where the Agent's Data Lives
docs.text:
Lab 2 asked three questions about the trace store: where does it live, who can read it, and how long is it kept. Ask them of every copy.

Copy Where Who can read it here How long Patient records The shared workshop EHR. Each seat has its own copy of the 12 patients, saved to IBM Cloud Object Storage. Anyone who sends your tenant ID. Your tools send it in a header with every request. Until the workshop environment is torn down Model context Each LLM call. Your agent uses Claude Sonnet 5.5. Orchestrate's model gateway sends each call to the workshop's model proxy, which forwards it to Anthropic's API. Anthropic, during the call (and the workshop proxy, which passes it through without storing it) Check your model provider's data-retention terms before sending it PHI. Traces The Orchestrate instance Every seat (Lab 2) 30 days Conversations The Orchestrate instance Administrators and builders in the tenant 30 days by default, up to 365 Concerns data/agent_output.json on your laptop Anyone with your laptop Until you delete them

docs.title: What IBM documents about storage on Orchestrate
docs.text:
These are IBM's statements for watsonx Orchestrate SaaS. Where IBM's pages don't cover something, the table says so. The pages below were read in October 2026.

Guarantee What IBM documents Source Region Orchestrate SaaS runs in several regions "to support data residency": on IBM Cloud, Dallas, Washington DC (Premium only), Toronto, São Paulo, London, Frankfurt, Paris, Tokyo and Sydney, plus four AWS regions. The page doesn't state that customer data stays in its region. Regional availability Encryption at rest All stored data is encrypted with AES-256, using AWS Key Management Service with AWS-managed keys. Storage is Amazon RDS and Amazon S3. Customer-managed keys aren't mentioned. Security, privacy, and data protection Encryption in transit TLS 1.2 or higher for all internal and external communication. Security, privacy, and data protection Isolation between customers Logical isolation between tenants on every plan. The Premium edition adds dedicated storage isolation. An existing instance can't be upgraded to it; you create a new Premium tenant and migrate. Data isolation Access inside a tenant Each user's chat history is isolated by user ID. Administrators and builders can view all conversations, metrics and traces in the tenant. Chat privacy, Monitoring agents Retention Chat history: 30 to 365 days, 30 by default. Agent analytics traces: 30 days. Workflow runs: 30 days. Data is deleted automatically after that. Managing data retention Service logs Operational logs don't contain customer content or message content. This is about IBM's service logs. Traces are a separate product feature, and they do contain content. Security, privacy, and data protection HIPAA The pricing page lists a "HIPAA-ready option" on the Premium plan only. The data isolation page says data isolation on AWS is currently available only on HIPAA-compliant clusters. We found no HIPAA statement for other plans, and no Business Associate Agreement terms for Orchestrate. Pricing, Data isolation Other certifications SOC 2, ISO 27001 and similar certifications aren't listed on the Orchestrate pages above. Not documented there

None of this changes what you saw in Lab 2. Encryption and tenant isolation protect the trace store from other customers. They don't decide who inside your tenant can read it. In this workshop, that's everyone.

Discuss

You're about to put this agent in front of real patient data. Using the tables above:

  1. Which plan would you need, and what would you ask IBM for in writing before signing?
  2. Who in your organization should hold a role that can read traces? Who shouldn't?
  3. Is 30 days of trace retention too long, too short, or right for your policy? It's fixed, so what would you do if it's wrong?
  4. Which copy of the data would you remove first? (Lab 2's answer: the trace copy, by having the tools return less.)

docs.title: Look at a Trace: What Can Your Agent Reach?
docs.text:
Open one of your agent's traces in Analyze, as in Lab 2. Find a run that called list_patients or get_inbox. If you can't find one, run the agent on patient-005 (Elena Vasquez). One of her messages asks about her neighbor Patricia Kowalski, who is also a patient. Check whether the agent looked her up.

Look at the tool output:

  • list_patients returns every patient in the practice: ID, name, birth date and active conditions.
  • get_inbox returns unanswered messages for all patients: patient name, subject, the full message body, date and category.
  • get_patient_record and get_messages take any patient ID. Nothing checks it against the patient the agent was asked about.

So your agent can read every patient's data while reviewing one. Lab 1 left the tools this way on purpose. The question is where to put the check.

Ask Bob

Open lab1/agent/tools.py and ask Bob: "Which of these tools take a patient_id that the model chooses, and which return data about every patient? What would each one need to know to refuse a request?"

docs.title: Why the Data Layer, Not the Prompt or the UI
docs.text:
There are four places you could enforce a rule like "Rachel Torres can't see Dr. Kim's concerns":

  • In the prompt. "Only discuss patients the user is authorized for." A prompt is a request to a model. Text in a patient's message can try to override it, and it does nothing about code that reads the store directly.
  • In the UI. Hide the rows the user shouldn't see. An API endpoint, an export script, a debug tool or next quarter's new feature all skip the filter.
  • In the application's queries. Every query includes WHERE provider_id = :provider_id. Forget it once and data leaks without an error.
  • In the data layer. The store enforces the rule on every read and write, whichever code path asks.

Only the data layer applies the rule to every code path, including code written next year.

docs.title: How you'd enforce this in your own database
docs.text:
Illustration: row-level security in PostgreSQL

This workshop doesn't run a database. If your concerns lived in PostgreSQL, a row-level security (RLS) policy would filter every query by the caller. From lab4/db/init.sql in the repository:

ALTER TABLE concerns ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY provider_concern_access ON concerns
    FOR ALL
    USING (
        provider_id = current_setting('app.provider_id', true)
        OR id IN (
            SELECT concern_id FROM shared_concerns
            WHERE shared_with = current_setting('app.provider_id', true)
        )
    );

A provider sees a concern only if their agent created it or someone shared it with them. Here the application sets app.provider_id, so a bug that sets the wrong ID still leaks data. In production the clinician signs in, that identity maps to a database role, and the policy checks the role.

The same idea applies to the EHR. The tools should ask the EHR for data as the clinician, and the EHR should refuse what that clinician can't see.

docs.title: Patterns for Protecting Agent Data
docs.text: None of these are specific to agents. An agent creates new sensitive data quickly, from many sources, on someone else's behalf, so you need all of them before its output reaches a real store.

docs.title: Default deny, explicit grant
docs.text: Nobody sees a concern unless they own it. Sharing writes a grant that records who shared what, with whom, and when. Access is the exception, and every exception leaves a record.

docs.title: Least-privilege credentials
docs.text: Give the agent's tools their own credential, limited to the data and operations they use. Keep reporting, migrations and admin work on separate credentials. Keep credentials in a secrets manager or the platform's connection store. Your Lab 1 tools read the EHR address and tenant from an Orchestrate connection for this reason.

docs.title: Encryption at rest and in transit
docs.text: Use TLS on every hop and encrypt every store, its backups and its exports. On Orchestrate, IBM documents this for the platform's own storage (see the table above). You're responsible for the stores you add: the EHR, the concerns store, and any exports.

docs.title: Audit logging of who read what
docs.text:
Record every read and write of PHI: which clinician, which patient, when, through which path, including denied requests. HIPAA's Security Rule requires audit controls. Keep the audit log append-only and separate from the data it describes.

Orchestrate's traces are built for debugging the agent, and they're very good at it. They aren't an audit log: every builder in the tenant can read them, they're kept for a fixed 30 days, and they record the agent's work, not the clinician's identity. Keep a separate audit log for that.

docs.title: Retention and deletion
docs.text: Decide how long concerns live, and delete them when the period ends. Copies also sit in traces, conversations, caches, backups and exports. Each one needs its own retention rule, and on a hosted platform some of those rules are set by the platform.

docs.title: Keep the clinician's identity attached end to end
docs.text:
The agent acts on someone's behalf. If its tools use one shared credential, the only thing between a prompt injection and another patient's record is the model's judgment. If every tool call carries the clinician's identity to the data layer, and the data layer checks it, the agent can only fetch what that clinician could fetch.

sequenceDiagram
    actor C as Rachel Torres
    participant UI as Inbox UI
    participant A as Agent
    participant T as Tool
    participant D as Data store
    C->>UI: Signs in, opens patient-005
    UI->>A: Review patient-005 for Rachel Torres
    Note over A: A message mentions patient-009,<br/>who isn't on Rachel Torres's panel
    A->>T: get_patient_record("patient-009")
    T->>D: Read patient-009 as Rachel Torres
    D-->>T: Denied (not her patient)
    T-->>A: Access denied
    A-->>UI: Concerns for patient-005 only

Two rules make this work:

  • The identity comes from the session. The model must not choose who it's acting as. If a tool takes the user's identity as an argument the model fills in, a prompt injection can change it.
  • The check happens below the agent. The model can be talked into asking for anything. The data layer decides what it gets.

The same identity should decide who can read the traces of that run. Lab 2 showed that today it doesn't: the trace of Rachel Torres's run would be readable by every builder in the tenant.

docs.title: How This Maps to Today's Workshop
docs.text:
This workshop is a simulation

The patients are synthetic. Here's where the ideas above show up in what you used.

  • Your patients are separate from everyone else's. The shared EHR keeps each seat's copy apart, keyed to a tenant ID derived from your API key, and saves each copy to Object Storage. The server enforces the separation. But the tenant ID separates seats, not clinicians, and your tools send it from a connection, so anyone with the value can use it. A real record system would authenticate each user (for example with SMART on FHIR) and check that identity on every request.
  • Your tools can read every patient. You saw this in the trace above. There's no per-patient scoping and no clinician identity.
  • Your traces hold raw tool output. Lab 2's masking layers clean the user's input and the agent's answer. The tool output stays in the trace. Returning fewer fields from the tools is the only layer that keeps PHI out of the trace.
  • Your concerns live in a JSON file on your laptop. No access control, no audit log, no retention rule.
  • Everyone shares one Orchestrate instance with broad roles. That let the whole room get running in minutes. A real deployment gives each team its own instance and each person only the role they need, including who can read traces.

docs.title: Taking It to Production
docs.text:
• Real authentication. Each clinician signs in, and that identity flows through the agent to the data layer.
  • Scoped tools. Each tool checks the requested patient against the identity of the caller, and the data layer checks again. The directory and inbox tools return only the clinician's own patients.
  • Minimal tool output. Tools return only what the agent needs, so less PHI reaches the model provider and the trace store.
  • Trace access and retention. Limit the roles that can read traces, decide whether 30 days fits your policy, and treat trace exports as PHI.
  • The right plan and paperwork. Confirm in writing which Orchestrate plan, region and agreements cover PHI before real data goes in.
  • Stable concerns. Give each concern an ID that survives re-runs, so an audit entry, a share grant or a retention rule can point at it. The repository's lab4/agent/ (from the open-source edition) shows one way: pass the previous concerns to the agent and update by ID.
Extra credit

Write down how you'd pass the clinician's identity from the inbox UI to the tools on Orchestrate. IBM documents context variables, which let the caller send values such as a user ID with a run so that the agent's tools can read them. We haven't tested them in this workshop. Ask Bob: "If each run of my Orchestrate agent carried the clinician's ID, how would get_patient_record in lab1/agent/tools.py use it, and what would the EHR have to check?"

docs.title: What Did We Learn?
docs.text: Principle What it means here Agent output is PHI Concerns get the same protection as the records they come from Know every copy EHR, model context, traces, conversations, concerns: each has a location, readers and a retention period Platform guarantees have limits Encryption and tenant isolation protect you from other customers, not from users inside your tenant Access control in the data layer One policy filters every query, whatever code path asks Default deny, explicit grant Nobody sees a concern by default; sharing leaves a record Identity end to end The clinician's identity, not the model, decides what the tools can fetch and who can read the trace Minimize at the source Data a tool never returns can't leak from the model, the trace or the answer

docs.title: Workshop Complete
docs.text:
Lab Problem Solution Lab 1 No structure, no tools, just vibes A ReAct agent with structured output Lab 2 No visibility into agent behavior Orchestrate traces, PII controls and plug-ins Lab 3 Hallucinations, overstepping, shallow investigation Evaluation: grounding checks, LLM-as-judge, critic Lab 4 Unrestricted data access Security: where the data lives, who can read it, identity end to end You're done!

You've built an agent, read its traces, checked its work, and worked through how to protect the data it reads and writes. See Additional Resources for further reading.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Complete these steps before the workshop to make sure your environment is ready.

docs.title: 1. IBM Cloud: log in
docs.text: The workshop runs on IBM Cloud. Your agent is deployed to watsonx Orchestrate. Your code talks to IBM Cloud with an API key: a long secret string that acts on your behalf. You'll create it in step 3, right before the installer asks for it.

1. Open the login link from your instructor.
