docs.title: Create your API key
docs.text:
Keep Bob open, and in your browser at cloud.ibm.com:

  1. In the top menu bar, open the Manage dropdown and choose Access (IAM).
  2. In the IAM menu on the left, find the Manage identities heading and click API keys underneath it.
  3. Click Create.
  4. Give the key a name, such as ai-agents-workshop, and click Create.
  5. Click Copy to copy the key. Leave this browser tab open until the installer has accepted it.

You only see the key once

IBM Cloud shows the key only when you create it. If you close the dialog before the installer accepts it, delete that key and create a new one.

docs.title: Run the installer
docs.text:
In Bob's terminal from step 2 (on Windows, the Bob window connected to WSL), run:

curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/obuzek/ai-agents-workshop/txc-2026-ibm/scripts/install.sh | bash

You don't need Homebrew or a preinstalled Python. The installer:

  1. Installs git, tar and gzip if they're missing (on Fedora that's usually just git), using your package manager with sudo, which may ask for your Linux password.
  2. Installs uv, which also downloads Python 3.12 for the workshop.
  3. Downloads the workshop into ~/ai-agents-workshop.
  4. Installs the workshop's Python packages.
  5. Installs the watsonx Orchestrate command-line tool, orchestrate, with uv tool install ibm-watsonx-orchestrate. uv puts it in ~/.local/bin and adds that folder to your PATH.
  6. Asks for your API key and connects you to IBM Cloud.
  7. Checks the setup.

It's safe to run again at any time: it skips what's already done and updates the workshop files.

docs.title: Paste your API key
docs.text:
When the installer reaches [6/7] Connect to IBM Cloud, paste the key you copied in the browser and press Enter. Nothing appears as you paste; that's on purpose. The script checks the key with IBM Cloud, finds the workshop's watsonx Orchestrate instance, saves your settings to .env, and connects the orchestrate CLI. Then it checks the whole setup.

You'll see:

[6/7] Connect to IBM Cloud
Created .env from .env-example
Paste your IBM Cloud API key (it won't show as you paste), then press Enter:
✓ API key works: <your workshop username> (account <account id>)
✓ Found your watsonx Orchestrate instance: <instance name>

docs.title: 4. Start the EHR inbox
docs.text:
The workshop uses a simulated Electronic Health Record (EHR) inbox, a patient portal for Lakeview Family Medicine. Start it from the workshop folder:

cd ~/ai-agents-workshop
uv run streamlit run app/ui.py --server.port 8501

The EHR API server starts automatically in the background on port 8000. Open http://localhost:8501 in your browser (on Windows, your normal Windows browser). You'll see:

  • A patient dropdown at the top (12 patients, some with unread messages)
  • Medical records with tabs for Conditions, Medications, Labs, History
  • A Concerns panel. It says your agent isn't running yet and Run Agent is disabled; each lab starts its agent in a second terminal.
  • An Inbox with patient messages and a conversation viewer

Each page takes about a second to load, because it fetches from the cloud.

Your patients live in the shared workshop EHR

The patient records come from one EHR server shared by the whole workshop. You get your own copy of the 12 patients, tied to your API key. Replies you send are visible only to you and your agent. If you create a new API key and run scripts/ibm_cloud_login.py again, you start over with a fresh copy.

Port 8501 or 8000 already in use?

Pick other ports:

API_PORT=9000 uv run streamlit run app/ui.py --server.port 9501

docs.title: 5. Verify it works
docs.text:
Leave the inbox running. In a second terminal, run the setup check:

cd ~/ai-agents-workshop
uv run python scripts/check_setup.py

It changes nothing. It prints the same list you saw at the end of the installer: one ✓ or ✗ per part of the setup, and for each ✗ a line starting with Fix: that says what to do.

You're ready when every line has a ✓ and you can browse patients and read their messages in the inbox.

Every agent has one, and each choice changes what can go wrong.  <table style="font-size:0.75em;margin-top:0.6em"> <tr><th style="text-align:left">Design question</th><th style="text-align:left">One end</th><th style="text-align:left">The other end</th></tr> <tr><td>Who starts it?</td><td>A person asks</td><td>An event or a schedule</td></tr> <tr><td>What can it do?</td><td>Read and suggest</td><td>Act on its own</td></tr> <tr><td>What comes back?</td><td>Free text</td><td>A structured result with fixed fields</td></tr> <tr><td>Where does it land?</td><td>A new chat window</td><td>The tools people already use</td></tr> <tr><td>Who decides?</td><td>The agent</td><td>The person</td></tr> </table>  <p style="margin-top:1em">Today: a background agent that reads, suggests and files structured concerns. The doctor decides.</p>  Note: Before the details: what is an agentic interface?  It's wherever people and an agent meet. A chat box is one kind. It's not the only kind.  Each row is a choice you make when you design one. Who kicks it off. What it's allowed to do. What shape its answer takes. Where that answer shows up. And who has the final say.  Those choices decide your risks. A chatbot anyone can type into has a very different attack surface from a background agent that writes into a fixed format.  Today we sit toward the right-hand column on most rows, and the doctor makes the call.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="todays-modules" -->  ## Today's modules  <div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:auto auto 1fr;gap:0.7em 1em;align-items:baseline;font-size:0.78em;margin-top:0.6em"> <div style="font-size:1.6em;font-weight:300;color:#0f62fe">1</div><div><strong>Build</strong></div><div>An agent on Orchestrate: definition, tools, deploy</div> <div style="font-size:1.6em;font-weight:300;color:#0f62fe">2</div><div><strong>Observe</strong></div><div>Traces, and why traces are PHI. Controls and plug-ins for PII</div> <div style="font-size:1.6em;font-weight:300;color:#0f62fe">3</div><div><strong>Improve</strong></div><div>Checks: grounding, LLM-as-judge and a critic, as judge agents</div> <div style="font-size:1.6em;font-weight:300;color:#0f62fe">4</div><div><strong>Secure</strong></div><div>Agent output is sensitive data. Data storage guarantees. Identity end to end (discussion)</div> </div>  <p style="font-size:0.7em;opacity:0.75;margin-top:2em">Labs 1–3: run it, then look at what changed. Lab 4: a discussion.</p>  Note: Here's the plan. In Lab 1 you deploy an agent to Orchestrate. In Lab 2 we look at its traces. They're full of patient data, so we'll look at what Orchestrate can mask, and what it can't. In Lab 3 we add checks on the agent's output, using other agents as judges. Lab 4 is a discussion: where does the agent's output get stored, and who gets to see it?  ---  <!-- .slide: id="section-agents" data-background="#0f62fe" -->  <div style="color:#fff">  <p style="font-size:0.65em;text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:0.12em;opacity:0.7">Section 1</p>  # The World of Agents  </div>  Note: Welcome!  When I first submitted this talk several months back, the world of agents was quite different. At that time, people were talking deeply about agent architectures, and "how to build an agent" was still esoteric for most people.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="sudo-make-agent" -->  <p style="text-align: center"> <img src="https://imgs.xkcd.com/comics/sandwich.png"/></br><code>$ sudo make me an agent</code></p>  Note: Since that time, the world changed. Between November and February, coding models took a massive leap forward, and now - the easiest way to make an agent is just to tell a coding model to make you one.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="what-is-an-agent" -->  ## What is an agent?  <div style="display: flex; gap: 2em"> <div style="flex: 1"> <ul><li>Prompt</li> <li>Tools</li> <li>Data</li> <li>Reasoning</li> <li>Repeat</li> </ul> </div>   <div style="flex: 1">   <h3>ReAct Loop</h3>   <svg viewBox="0 0 320 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-height:200px;margin-top:0.5em">     <defs>       <marker id="react-arr" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="7" refX="9" refY="3.5" orient="auto">         <polygon points="0 0, 10 3.5, 0 7" fill="#888"/>       </marker>     </defs>     <line x1="183" y1="87" x2="225" y2="153" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#react-arr)"/>     <line x1="204" y1="190" x2="116" y2="190" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#react-arr)"/>     <line x1="95" y1="153" x2="137" y2="87" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#react-arr)"/>     <circle cx="160" cy="50" r="42" fill="#0f62fe"/>     <text x="160" y="50" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="white" font-size="13" font-family="IBM Plex Sans, sans-serif">Observe</text>     <circle cx="248" cy="190" r="42" fill="#0f62fe"/>     <text x="248" y="190" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="white" font-size="13" font-family="IBM Plex Sans, sans-serif">Plan</text>     <circle cx="72" cy="190" r="42" fill="#0f62fe"/>     <text x="72" y="190" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="white" font-size="13" font-family="IBM Plex Sans, sans-serif">Act</text>   </svg>   </div> </div>  Note: I think we're close to not needing this anymore! But just to levelset:  ---  <!-- .slide: id="do-you-need-agent" -->  ## Do You Even Need To Make An Agent?  <img src="../images/subagents-screenshot.png"/>  Note: In fact, it's even simpler than that: now, general purpose agents can write themselves subagents on the fly, based on nothing more than a couple words. And those agents can launch agents, and those agents can launch agents...  ---  <!-- .slide: id="why-build-agent" -->  ## Do You Even Need To Make An Agent?  ### Why you might want to build an agent:  * You need to run a similar type of workflow over and over again * You work on sensitive data that can't be dropped into a general purpose LLM * You need to share your workflow with a large number of team members * You need that workflow to run reliably and efficiently  Note: So that brings us here - to the problem space of _responsible_ AI agents.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="why-were-here" -->  ## Why We're Here  ### Today You'll Learn:  1. How do you design an agent that needs to operate on sensitive data? 2. Given a user problem where your job is to build a tool that supports experts, how do you make sure you support instead of replacing their expertise? 3. Which tools are the right ones to get started with agents?  ---  <!-- .slide: id="responsible-agent" -->  ## What Does It Mean For An Agent To Be Responsible?  <div style="display: flex; gap: 2em"> <div style="flex: 1">   <h3>Qualities of Responsibility</h3>   <ul>     <li><strong>Augments human intelligence</strong>: Reduces time spent completing tasks</li>     <li><strong>Aligns with human values</strong>: Follows human values, ethical considerations, guidelines    and policies - necessary in critical organizations</li>     <li><strong>Robust</strong>: Behaves predictably in complex environments</li>     <li><strong>Efficient</strong>: Doesn't waste computation achieving its goals</li>     <li><strong>Private</strong>: Doesn't reveal information except to those who should have access</li>     <li><strong>Explainable</strong>: Humans can reason about the agent's behavior</li>   </ul> </div> <div style="flex: 1">   <h3>Impacts to Consider</h3>   <ul>     <li><strong>Human Dignity</strong>: Workers should see AI as partners, not replacements for their skills</li>     <li><strong>Human Agency</strong>: Agents should only make decisions that keep human critical thinking intact</li>     <li><strong>Jobs</strong> Augmenting, instead of replacing, creates opportunities for more people to create new things</li>     <li><strong>Environment</strong>: Computational efficiency matters</li>   </ul> </div> </div>  <p class="push-bottom" style="text-align: right; font-size: 0.6em">source: <a href="https://www.ibm.com/granite/docs/resources/ai-agents-opportunities-risks-and-mitigations.pdf">AI Agents: Opportunities, Risks and Mitigations</a></p>  Note: We can frame this a few different ways.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="responsible-agent-articles" -->  ## What Does It Mean For An Agent To Be Responsible?  <div style="overflow: hidden; height: 600px; border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.2); border-radius: 4px;">   <img src="../images/lee-2025-ai-critical-thinking.pdf.png"        style="width: 100%; height: 100%; object-fit: cover; object-position: top; display: block;"/> </div>  Note: This study from Lee et al. at CHI 2025 found that mechanizing routine tasks, and leaving exception handling to the user, actually makes the user's judgment worse since they're no longer practicing with regularity, and they are then less prepared when exceptions arise.  Users with AI access produced a less diverse set of outcomes for the same task — interpreted as deterioration of critical thinking  This has also long been a lesson of autopilot automation in aviation: The Air France disaster in 2009, where pilots couldn't fly a plane on autopilot. Now - pilots must hand-fly regularly to prevent skill erosion.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="useful-agent" -->  ## What Does It Mean For An Agent To Be Useful?  <div style="display: flex; gap: 2em"> <div style="flex: 1">   <h3>Antipatterns</h3>   <ul>     <li><strong>Sparkle button</strong>: Implies "magic"; usually isn't</li>     <li><strong>Unnecessarily broad chat</strong>: McDonald's doesn't need to generate Python code</li>     <li><strong>Deterministic workflow made probabilistic</strong>: Simple workflows should stay simple</li>     <li><strong>Limited, by accident</strong>: Hasn't thought through the user's actual needs</li>   </ul> </div> <div style="flex: 1">   <p/> </div> </div>  Note: Wearable app that generates charts for you, but wants you to do it in plain text instead of buttons.  A grammar checker that responds to your friends, replacing your relationships with them.  McDonald's chat, so unrestricted that it can write Python for you.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="problem-statement"-->  ### The Problem  Since the introduction of **EHR portals**, doctors are **overwhelmed with messages** from their patients. Sometimes the patients ask several questions in one message. Sometimes the messages are urgent. Responding to them comes on top of a doctor's patient load — and that means that **keeping up is exhausting**. But when patients don't get responses to their questions, they may let **important medical needs go un-handled**.  ### The Question  Can we use an AI agent to support doctor-patient communication outside of appointments in a way that:  * preserves the doctor-patient relationship, * enables the doctor to remain the expert, and * reduces the cognitive load of keeping up with their inbox?  Note: Can we build an agent that does this, and still helps the doctors?  ---  <!-- .slide: id="our-approach" -->  ## Our Approach  The recipe for a responsible healthcare inbox agent:  * Never drafts for the doctor * Never offers medical advice * DOES help summarize information * DOES help extract information * DOES help surface information  ---  <!-- .slide: id="our-approach-2" -->  ## Our Approach  The UI:  <table style="font:1.2em"> <tr><td><h3>What</h3></td><td><h3>Why</h3></td></tr> <tr><td>Skips the chatbox approach</td><td>Limits the possible workflows the agent enables</td></tr> <tr><td>Backgrounds the agent</td><td>Prevents feedback loops on jailbreaking and prompt injection while still accomplishing our needs</td></tr> </table>  Our agent will: * Extract important points from messages and labs * Raise those points in a structured way * Expose them to the user without breaking confidentiality laws  <a href="http://localhost:8501">Our "Electronic Health Record"</a>  ---  <!-- .slide: id="adlc-intro" -->  ## What is the ADLC?  The Agent Development Lifecycle (ADLC) describes the end-to-end process for designing, building, and operating AI systems responsibly.  <p style="text-align: center"><img style="width: 75%; display: block; margin: 0 auto;" src="../images/adlc-diagram.png"/></p>  - Structured approach to AI system development - Incorporates governance and ethics at every phase - Enables repeatable, auditable workflows  Note: A few versions of this have emerged.   <p class="push-bottom" style="text-align: right; font-size: 0.6em">source: <a href="https://www.ibm.com/forms/mkt-whitepaper-f42e50">Architecting secure enterprise AI agents with MCP</a></p>  ---  <!-- .slide: id="adlc-phase-1" data-visibility="hidden" -->  ## Phase 1: Problem Definition  - Identify business need and success criteria - Assess feasibility and data availability - Define scope, constraints, and stakeholders - Conduct ethical impact assessment  Note: The problem definition phase is often undervalued. Ethical impact assessment here prevents costly redesigns later.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="adlc-phase-2" data-visibility="hidden" -->  ## Phase 2: Data Collection & Preparation  - Identify and gather relevant data sources - Clean, label, and validate data - Address bias and representativeness - Establish data governance and lineage  ---  <!-- .slide: id="adlc-phase-3" data-visibility="hidden" -->  ## Phase 3: Model Development  - Select model architecture and approach - Train, fine-tune, or prompt-engineer - Evaluate performance and safety metrics - Iterate based on results  ---  <!-- .slide: id="adlc-phase-4" data-visibility="hidden" -->  ## Phase 4: Deployment & Integration  - Package and serve the model - Integrate with existing systems and workflows - Set up monitoring and alerting - Define rollback and incident response plans  ---  <!-- .slide: id="adlc-phase-5" data-visibility="hidden" -->  ## Phase 5: Operations & Governance  - Monitor model performance over time - Detect and address drift and degradation - Maintain audit trails and documentation - Periodic re-evaluation and retraining  ---  <!-- .slide: id="adlc-agents" -->  ## ADLC for Agents  Agent-based systems introduce additional considerations:  - **Tool access** — what can the agent do? - **Autonomy level** — when does it act without human approval? - **Memory & state** — what persists across sessions? - **Observability** — can you explain what the agent did and why?  Note: These four dimensions map directly to the four labs: build, observe, improve, secure.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="watsonx-products" -->  ## watsonx.ai Studio vs watsonx Orchestrate vs watsonx.governance  <div style="display:flex;gap:28px;font-size:0.78em;line-height:1.4"> <div style="flex:1;border-top:4px solid #8d8d8d;padding-top:0.6em"> <p style="margin:0 0 0.2em;font-weight:600;font-size:1.25em">watsonx.ai Studio</p> <p style="margin:0 0 0.8em;opacity:0.75">"A studio of integrated tools for building generative AI and machine learning solutions"</p> <p style="margin:0 0 0.3em"><strong>What it's for</strong></p> <ul style="margin:0 0 0.8em 1em"> <li>Foundation models: IBM and open source</li> <li>Prompt Lab: experiment with prompts</li> <li>Projects: shared workspaces for assets</li> <li>Tuning, RAG, deployments</li> </ul> <p style="margin:0 0 0.3em"><strong>Today</strong></p> <p style="margin:0">You open it once. That creates the watsonx profile that governance needs.</p> </div> <div style="flex:1;border-top:4px solid #0f62fe;padding-top:0.6em"> <p style="margin:0 0 0.2em;font-weight:600;font-size:1.25em">watsonx Orchestrate</p> <p style="margin:0 0 0.8em;opacity:0.75">"An agent management platform designed to help build, deploy, orchestrate, manage and govern AI agents"</p> <p style="margin:0 0 0.3em"><strong>What it's for</strong></p> <ul style="margin:0 0 0.8em 1em"> <li>Agents and the tools they call</li> <li>Connections that hold credentials</li> <li>Controls and plug-ins: guardrails, PII</li> <li>Traces and evaluation</li> </ul> <p style="margin:0 0 0.3em"><strong>Today</strong></p> <p style="margin:0">Where you build and run your agent: definition, tools, connection, controls, traces.</p> </div> <div style="flex:1;border-top:4px solid #8d8d8d;padding-top:0.6em"> <p style="margin:0 0 0.2em;font-weight:600;font-size:1.25em">watsonx.governance</p> <p style="margin:0 0 0.8em;opacity:0.75">"Govern any AI, anywhere with real-time visibility, enterprise controls, and continuous accountability"</p> <p style="margin:0 0 0.3em"><strong>What it's for</strong></p> <ul style="margin:0 0 0.8em 1em"> <li>Evaluating and monitoring AI output</li> <li>Metrics, factsheets, model history</li> <li>AI risk management</li> <li>Policy and regulatory compliance</li> </ul> <p style="margin:0 0 0.3em"><strong>Today</strong></p> <p style="margin:0">The evaluation concepts behind Lab 3: grounding, judges, metrics.</p> </div> </div>  Note: You'll hear about three watsonx products today. watsonx.ai Studio is where you work with models directly, try prompts in Prompt Lab, and keep things in projects. Today you only open it once. Opening it creates the watsonx profile that governance needs.  watsonx Orchestrate is where your agent lives. The agent, its tools, its connection to the EHR, the controls on it, and the traces of every run are all in Orchestrate.  watsonx.governance is for evaluating and monitoring AI, and for managing risk. In Lab 3 we build the kind of checks it's designed to track: grounding, judges, metrics.  Sources (IBM's own descriptions): - watsonx.ai: https://www.ibm.com/products/watsonx-ai and https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/watsonx/saas?topic=overview-watsonx ("a studio of integrated tools…", Prompt Lab, projects) - Prompt Lab and projects: https://dataplatform.cloud.ibm.com/docs/content/wsj/getting-started/get-started-prompt-lab.html?context=wx - watsonx Orchestrate: https://www.ibm.com/products/watsonx-orchestrate - watsonx.governance: https://www.ibm.com/products/watsonx-governance and https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/watsonx/saas?topic=overview-watsonx (evaluate prompts, monitor output, factsheets, risk)  ---  <!-- .slide: id="which-model" -->  ## Which model?  Today's agent runs on **Claude Sonnet 5.5**. It's a high-end model at a reasonable cost.  - In Orchestrate it's `virtual-model/anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5`, reached through Orchestrate's model gateway. - Orchestrate can be set up with many model backends: watsonx.ai, Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Ollama and others. - Through watsonx.ai you can choose open-weights models, or deploy your own. That's one way to run on-prem.  Note: We're using Claude Sonnet 5.5 today because it's a strong model at a reasonable price. We tried the free gpt-oss-120b first. It often stopped after one look at the patient record, so it missed things.  You're not locked into one model. Orchestrate's model gateway can talk to a long list of providers. Most people encounter agents as **chat agents** — you type, the agent responds. For our doctor inbox, that's the wrong choice.  With a chat box, there's nothing stopping a doctor from asking the agent to draft a reply, confirm a diagnosis, or "just handle it." The UI is a constraint on behavior. Choose it intentionally.  A **background agent** is triggered by data arriving — a new patient message — processes it, and writes structured output to a store the doctor then reads. The agent's role is constrained by design, not by a warning in the prompt.  <a href="http://localhost:8501">Open the EHR →</a>  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab1-why-orchestrate" -->  ## Lab 1: Why Orchestrate? The agent decides which tools to call and in what order — we don't script that.  The doctor never sees raw LLM output. The agent fills in a typed `Concern`:  - `title`, `summary`, `action` — what the doctor needs to act on - `concern_type` — medication, lab result, symptom, follow-up, administrative - `urgency` — routine, soon, or urgent - `evidence` — specific values and dates, not paraphrases - `related` — links back to the relevant messages, labs, encounters  The contract between agent and UI is explicit. The UI renders the schema. That's the constraint.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab1-structured-output" -->  ## Lab 1: Structured Outputs ≠ "Please Return JSON"  LLMs generate one token at a time. Some inference services offer **constrained decoding** (the server masks tokens that would break the schema). It's the difference between asking someone to drive the speed limit and installing a speed governor.  Without it, we recommend: **prompt with the schema, validate, retry once.**  - `deploy.py` builds the JSON schema from `models.py` and adds it to the agent's instructions - `agent.py` checks every answer against the Pydantic model, and retries once with the error  For a background agent with no human watching, this isn't a nice-to-have. If the output doesn't parse at 3 AM, nobody finds out.  Quick test: `uv run python scripts/check_structured_outputs.py --patients 3 --skip-judges`  Note: Constrained decoding is something the inference server does. Our agent on Orchestrate doesn't have it, so our code does the checking. When we tested this agent on gpt-oss-120b, the model we started with, 20 of 24 answers were valid on the first try, and all 24 were valid after one retry. On Claude Sonnet 5.5, today's model, 10 of 12 were valid on the first try, and all 12 after one retry. The quick test runs your agent on three patients and prints the same numbers for your own agent. For agents, that's not enough.  When something goes wrong, you need to know which tools the agent called, in what order, with what inputs, and what the LLM actually saw before it decided. You need the **content**, not just the metadata.  That creates a tension: the richer your traces, the more useful they are for debugging — and the more likely they are to contain sensitive data. Your trace store becomes a **secondary repository of PHI** that needs its own governance posture.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab2-orchestrate-traces" -->  ## Lab 2: Traces in Orchestrate  Orchestrate traces every run of your agent. There's no code to add.  Each trace has:  - the run, from start to answer - every LLM call: model, input, output, token counts - every tool call: arguments and the full output  You can read traces in the Orchestrate UI, with `orchestrate observability traces` in the CLI, or through the API.  Traces show tokens, but not cost. To estimate cost, multiply tokens by the model's price.  Note: In the open-source edition, this lab is about adding tracing to the agent. Here it's already on. Run the agent on a patient, then open the trace and find your agent by its seat prefix. Look at what the tool returned. You'll see the whole patient record in there.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab2-traces-are-phi" -->  ## Lab 2: Traces Are PHI  Open a trace and look at the tool output. To log less, return less from your tools.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab2-what-traces-show" -->  ## Lab 2: What Traces Actually Show You  Traces show you things you can't see any other way:  - **Tool call order** — did the agent investigate, or stop after one call? - **The implicit summarization problem** — compare what tools returned (ground truth) to what the agent concluded. Discrepancies are visible by eye. Lab 3 automates catching them. - **The invisible prompt** — the doctor never sees the message the agent acted on. If the prompt is poorly written or biased, the trace is where you find out. - **Tokens per run** — at scale, "the agent runs on every patient every day" adds up fast.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab2-datasets" -->  ## Lab 2: Traces as Evaluation Data  Traces aren't just for debugging right now — they're raw material for getting better over time.  - Save good and bad runs as examples. Over time you have a set of real agent behavior to test new versions against. - When a clinician spots a wrong concern, record what went wrong. That's feedback from the domain expert to the engineering team.  And then there's **LLM-as-Judge**: use another LLM to check the agent's output at scale. We'll build this in Lab 3, from the same data you see in the trace.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="section-lab-3" data-background="#0f62fe" -->  <div style="color:#fff">  <p style="font-size:0.65em;text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:0.12em;opacity:0.7">Lab 3</p>  # Improving Your Agent  Use what you observed to make it better.  </div>  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab3-adlc-loop" -->  ## Lab 3: Where We Are in the ADLC  Lab 1 was Model Development — building the agent. Lab 2 was Operations — adding visibility. Lab 3 is the feedback loop between the two:  **Run agent → Inspect traces → Identify failure → Implement fix → Run agent**  This is the inner loop of the ADLC's Operations & Governance phase. Each improvement in this lab starts from something you can see in a trace.  Observability only pays off if you act on what you find.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab3-what-we-found" -->  ## Lab 3: What to Look For in the Traces  Things to check in your Lab 2 traces:  **1. Made-up evidence.** Compare the tool output (what the data says) to the agent's concerns (what it claims). Look for lab values or dates that aren't in the record.  **2. Off-task answers.** The instructions say not to make clinical recommendations. Look for suggested diagnoses or treatments anyway. A system prompt is a request, not a constraint.  **3. One big tool call.** `get_patient_record` returns the whole record — demographics, all conditions, all labs, all messages. Our agent usually calls it once and stops. More data in context means more chances to make things up.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab3-prompt-injection" -->  ## Lab 3: Prompt Injection — Reduced by Design  You might wonder whether a patient could craft a portal message to hijack the agent.  In this system, the risk is reduced by a deliberate architectural decision: the agent runs in the background, and its output goes to the **doctor** — not back to the patient. The patient never sees agent output, so there's no feedback loop to exploit.  The patient's message still reaches the agent, as tool output. Nothing on the platform checks tool output, so the agent's instructions and the doctor's review are what stand in the way.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab3-focused-tools" -->  ## Lab 3: Focused Tools Force Intentional Investigation  Replace `get_patient_record` with keyword-based search tools: `search_conditions`, `search_labs`, `search_medications`. The agent has to say what it's looking for before it gets any data.  Instead of drowning in everything at once, it has to reason first: "The patient mentioned fatigue — let me check thyroid conditions and TSH labs." This is investigation, not retrieval.  Fewer tokens in context means lower cost, less hallucination surface area, and less PHI in the traces.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab3-critic" -->  ## Lab 3: Checks as Judge Agents  Each check is its own agent on Orchestrate, with no tools and its own output schema:  1. **Claim extractor** — pulls out every specific, checkable medical claim in each concern. Vague descriptions ("recent lab results") are dropped. You can't check something that doesn't say anything specific.  2. **Grounding judge** (LLM-as-judge) — checks each claim against the patient's record. Is that lab value really there?  3. **Critic** — looks at the grounding results and whether the concern stays on task, and writes feedback for the agent.  Why extract claims first? The judge returns one verdict per claim, so you can tell *which part* of a concern is wrong.  Note: These three are prompts plus a schema, deployed as agents with no tools. You send each one a concern and the patient's data and get structured JSON back, checked the same way as in Lab 1.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab3-judge-bias" -->  ## Lab 3: Who Checks the Checker?  Our judges run on the same model as the agent: Claude Sonnet 5.5. A model checking its own kind of output has a bias. It tends to make the same mistakes it's looking for.  Ways to reduce it:  - a judge from a different model family (Orchestrate's catalog has more than one) - a model trained for the check, such as a groundedness detector - a clinician reviewing a sample of verdicts  Judges cut down on what reaches the doctor. The doctor is still the one who decides.  Note: In the open-source edition, there's an option to check grounding with Granite Guardian running locally. It's a model trained to detect ungrounded claims. We're not running it today. Here, the judge is the same model as the agent, so keep that bias in mind when you read its verdicts.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="section-lab-4" data-background="#0f62fe" -->  <div style="color:#fff">  <p style="font-size:0.65em;text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:0.12em;opacity:0.7">Lab 4</p>  # Securing Data  Who can read what the agent knows? A discussion.  </div>  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab4-output-is-sensitive" -->  ## Lab 4: Agent Output Is Sensitive Data  We've been protecting the patient records the agent reads. But the concerns the agent writes are also sensitive — they're clinical findings derived from patient data.  In Labs 1-3, the agent writes to a flat JSON file. Any code path can read or overwrite any patient's concerns. Run the agent twice and the first run's output is gone.  In a multi-provider practice, provider A's agent may reach a different conclusion about the same patient than provider B. That's clinically significant. Those conclusions need access control — and they need to be stable across runs.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab4-storage-guarantees" -->  ## Lab 4: Where Does the Agent's Data Live?  <table style="font-size:0.72em"> <tr><td><strong>Data</strong></td><td><strong>Stored in</strong></td><td><strong>What we saw today</strong></td></tr> <tr><td>Traces: tool output, LLM context</td><td>watsonx Orchestrate</td><td>every seat can read them, kept 30 days</td></tr> <tr><td>Agent, tools, connection</td><td>watsonx Orchestrate</td><td>credentials in the connection</td></tr> <tr><td>Patient records</td><td>shared EHR on Code Engine</td><td>a copy per tenant, keyed by a header</td></tr> <tr><td>Concerns</td><td>a JSON file on your laptop</td><td>no access control, no audit log</td></tr> </table>  Questions to ask your platform, for each one:  - Where is it stored, and in which region? - Who can read it? Can you limit that per user? - How long is it kept? How do you delete it, including backups and exports? - Is it encrypted at rest and in transit? Who holds the keys?  Note: Ask these about every place the agent's data ends up, including traces. Get the answers from the vendor's documentation. IBM's general watsonx data security statement says data at rest is encrypted by default, and that you can bring your own keys with Key Protect. That statement covers watsonx as a whole. The Orchestrate security page doesn't mention customer-managed keys, so check what applies to the specific service you use. For Orchestrate traces, what we saw in this account is that every seat can read them and they're kept for 30 days.  Sources: https://dataplatform.cloud.ibm.com/docs/content/wsj/getting-started/security-data.html?context=wx  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab4-data-layer" -->  ## Lab 4: Access Control Belongs in the Data Layer  You can put a rule like "Rachel Torres can't see Dr. Kim's concerns" in four places:  - **The prompt.** A request to the model. Text in a patient message can override it. - **The UI.** Every other path to the data skips it. - **The application's queries.** Forget the `WHERE` clause once, and data leaks. - **The data layer.** The store checks every read and write, whichever code asks.  For example, Postgres row-level security applies a policy to every query, including ones you haven't written yet. The default is deny. Sharing a concern writes an explicit grant, and that grant is a record you can audit.  Note: The repository has a Lab 4 schema with a row-level security policy if you want to read one. We're not running a database today. I want you to know the rule can live in one place, in the store.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab4-identity" -->  ## Lab 4: Identity End to End  The agent acts for a clinician. Its tools should fetch only what that clinician could fetch.  - **The identity comes from the session.** The model never fills it in. If it's a tool argument, a prompt injection can change it. - **The check happens below the agent.** The data layer decides what comes back.  Today, neither is true:  - Your tools send your tenant, which separates students. It doesn't identify a clinician. - Within your tenant, the tools can read any patient. `list_patients` and `get_inbox` return conditions and message subjects for every patient.  Note: Patient Elena Vasquez's message mentions her neighbor, Patricia Kowalski. Nothing today stops the agent from looking up Patricia's record while it reviews Elena. The Lab 4 code in the repository scopes tools to one patient, but even there the clinic directory tools return every patient's conditions. A real fix needs the clinician's identity checked in the record system.  ---  <!-- .slide: id="lab4-production" -->  ## Lab 4: In Production  - Each clinician signs in, with OAuth or SMART on FHIR, and that identity reaches the record system on every tool call - Concerns go in a store with access control by clinician, an audit log, and a retention rule - Traces get the same treatment: limit who can read them, minimize what goes in, and set how long they're kept - Credentials live in the platform's connections or a secrets manager, not in `.env` - Each team gets its own Orchestrate instance and only the roles it needs  ---  <!-- .slide: id="further-lifecycle" -->  ## Going further on watsonx  <style> .reveal .further { font-size: 0.95em; line-height: 1.35; } .reveal .further.detail { font-size: 0.9em; } .reveal .further .ok { color: #4589ff; font-weight: 600; } .reveal .further .unt { color: #8d8d8d; font-weight: 600; } .reveal .further .cols { display: flex; gap: 28px; } .reveal .further .col { flex: 1; min-width: 0; border-top: 4px solid #0f62fe; padding-top: 0.5em; } .reveal .further .step { margin: 0; font-weight: 600; font-size: 1.3em; } .reveal .further .q { margin: 0.15em 0 0.3em; font-style: italic; } .reveal .further .prod { margin: 0 0 0.7em; opacity: 0.7; font-size: 0.85em; } .reveal .further ul { list-style: none; margin: 0 !important; padding: 0 !important; display: block; } .reveal .further li { list-style: none; margin: 0 0 0.5em !important; padding-left: 1.2em; text-indent: -1.2em; } .reveal .further li::marker { content: none; } .reveal .further .legend { margin: 1.4em 0 0; font-size: 0.85em; } .reveal .further code { font-size: 0.9em; } </style>  <div class="further"> <div class="cols"> <div class="col"> <p class="step">1. Treat them as PHI.</li> <li><span class="unt">?</span> <strong>Agent monitoring:</strong> success rate, response time and tokens for agents deployed to production. Built on watsonx.governance.</li> <li><span class="unt">?</span> <strong>Model choice:</strong> watsonx.ai Studio has IBM and open-weights models, and you can deploy your own. Check again every time you change it.</p> </div> </div> <p class="legend"><span class="ok">✓ tested today</span>    <span class="unt">? documented by IBM, not tested here</span></p> </div>  Note: Constrain it. controls, plug-ins, and smaller tool output - Lab 3: focused tools; grounding and critic checks as judge agents - Lab 4: where agent data is stored, and identity end to end  </div> </div>  ---  <!-- .slide: id="responsible-by-design" -->  ## Responsible by Design  Responsibility isn't something you bolt on at the end.  - **Build** with constraints from day one — structure limits what the agent can say - **Observe** so you can explain every decision — and defend it - **Improve** using evidence from real traces, not intuition - **Secure** the data the agent reads and writes, in the data layer          <p>Jump to: Intro · ADLC · Lab 1 · Lab 2 · Lab 3 · Lab 4 · Wrap-up</p> <p>Keyboard shortcuts: <code>F</code> fullscreen · <code>O</code> overview · <code>S</code> speaker notes · <code>←</code> <code>→</code> navigate</p>

docs.title: Reference: Manual Tool-Calling Agent (No Framework)
docs.text: This is a reference implementation of a ReAct agent using the OpenAI API directly, without LangGraph or any agent framework. The workshop uses LangGraph, but this shows what's happening under the hood.

docs.title: The Agent Loop
docs.text:
The core loop: send messages to the LLM, check if it wants to call tools, execute them, feed results back, repeat until it responds with text.

"""
The naive agent — a ReAct tool-calling loop using the OpenAI API directly.

The agent receives a patient ID and a goal. It decides which tools to call,
in what order, and how to interpret the results. When it has gathered enough
information, it returns structured concerns.
"""

import json
import logging
import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from openai import OpenAI, RateLimitError

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENAI_BASE_URL from env
MODEL = os.environ.get("OPENAI_MODEL", "gpt-4o")
MAX_TURNS = 20  # safety limit on tool-calling rounds
MAX_RETRIES = 5  # retries on rate limit


def _llm_call(messages, tools):
    """Call the LLM with retry + exponential backoff on rate limits."""
    for attempt in range(MAX_RETRIES):
        try:
            return client.chat.completions.create(
                model=MODEL,
                messages=messages,
                tools=tools,
            )
        except RateLimitError:
            if attempt == MAX_RETRIES - 1:
                raise
            wait = 2 ** attempt
            logger.warning("Rate limited, retrying in %ds...", wait)
            time.sleep(wait)
    raise RuntimeError("Unreachable")


SYSTEM_PROMPT = """\
You are a clinical inbox assistant. Review the patient's record and surface
actionable concerns for the doctor.

When done investigating, respond with JSON matching the PatientConcerns schema.
"""


def process_patient(patient_id: str):
    """Run the agent loop for a single patient."""

    # TOOLS and TOOL_FUNCTIONS are defined separately — see below
    from tools import TOOLS, TOOL_FUNCTIONS

    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": f"Please review patient {patient_id}."},
    ]

    for turn in range(MAX_TURNS):
        response = _llm_call(messages, TOOLS)
        choice = response.choices[0]

        # If the model wants to call tools, execute them and feed results back
        if choice.finish_reason == "tool_calls":
            messages.append(choice.message.model_dump())

            for tool_call in choice.message.tool_calls:
                fn_name = tool_call.function.name
                fn_args = json.loads(tool_call.function.arguments)

                fn = TOOL_FUNCTIONS.get(fn_name)
                if fn is None:
                    result = {"error": f"Unknown tool: {fn_name}"}
                else:
                    try:
                        result = fn(**fn_args)
                    except Exception as e:
                        result = {"error": str(e)}

                messages.append({
                    "role": "tool",
                    "tool_call_id": tool_call.id,
                    "content": json.dumps(result, default=str),
                })

            continue

        # Model is done — parse the final JSON response
        raw = choice.message.content.strip()
        if raw.startswith("```"):
            lines = raw.split("\n")
            if lines[0].startswith("```"):
                lines = lines[1:]
            if lines and lines[-1].startswith("```"):
                lines = lines[:-1]
            raw = "\n".join(lines)

        return json.loads(raw)

    raise RuntimeError(f"Hit max turns ({MAX_TURNS}) without finishing")

docs.title: Tool Definitions
docs.text:
With the raw OpenAI API, you define tools twice: once as a Python function, and once as a JSON schema the LLM can read. LangGraph's @tool decorator eliminates this duplication.

# The function
def search_labs(patient_id: str, test_name: str) -> list[dict]:
    """Search for all results of a specific lab test across all dates."""
    record = get_patient_record(patient_id)
    matches = []
    for lab in record.get("labs", []):
        for panel in lab.get("panels", []):
            for result in panel.get("results", []):
                if test_name.lower() in result["test"].lower():
                    matches.append({
                        "date": lab["date"],
                        "test": result["test"],
                        "value": result["value"],
                        "unit": result.get("unit", ""),
                        "interpretation": result.get("interpretation", ""),
                    })
    return sorted(matches, key=lambda r: r["date"], reverse=True)


# The schema (you have to write this by hand)
TOOLS = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "search_labs",
            "description": "Search for all results of a specific lab test across all dates.",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "patient_id": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "description": "The patient ID, e.g. 'patient-001'",
                    },
                    "test_name": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "description": "Lab test name (case-insensitive partial match)",
                    },
                },
                "required": ["patient_id", "test_name"],
            },
        },
    },
]

# The dispatch table (you have to maintain this too)
TOOL_FUNCTIONS = {
    "search_labs": search_labs,
}
